Wadō 3 (710) | honden = Nagare-zukuri style | festival = July 15 | ceremonies = Kogashi Matsuri (July 15–16) }} The [[Kinomiya Shrine]] is located in [[Atami]], [[Shizuoka (city)|Shizuoka]], and is famous for its natural treasures, especially the historic trees within its grounds.{{Cite web |last=Author |first=No |date=1999-12-08 |title=The natural treasures of Kinomiya Shrine |url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/1999/12/08/environment/the-natural-treasures-of-kinomiya-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-19 |website=The Japan Times |language=en}} It is located near [[Kinomiya Station]],{{Cite web |title=Expand your life expectancy at Kinomiya shrine, in Atami city｜TOMO – 供TOMO 玄米コーヒーオンラインストア |url=https://tomo.life/en/blogs/shinto-and-shrines/lets-visit-kinomiya-shrine |access-date=2023-10-19 |website=tomo.life}} and serves [[Amazake]]. [[File:Cinnamomum camphora 20100612 (Kinomiya Shrine) (B).jpg|thumb|The large camphor tree of Azusawake Jinja]] [[File:Cinnamomum camphora 20100612 (Kinomiya Shrine) (2nd).jpg|thumb|The second large camphor tree]] '''Kinomiya Jinja''' is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Atami|ja|熱海市|lt=Atami City}}, {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|ja|静岡県|lt=Shizuoka Prefecture}}, Japan. Under the modern shrine Rank system, it was once a village shrine. == Shrine name == Historically known as “Kimiya Myōjin” or “Kinomiya Daimyōjin,” among others. After the Meiji Restoration, it was identified as the “Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja” (阿豆佐和気命神社) as a result of being associated with a Shikinaisha of that name. Later, when it was found that this was incorrect, it reverted to its current name.{{efn|However, pamphlets distributed by the shrine still state, “It is recorded in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō as ‘Azusawake Jinja.’”}} {{efn|Other candidates for Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja include a shrine of the same name in Toshima Village, Tokyo.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=http://www.tokyo-jinjacho.or.jp/tosho/2843/|title=Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja|publisher=Tokyo Jinja-chō|accessdate=2021-04-21}}}} == Enshrined Deities == * Yamato Takeru no Mikoto * Iitakeru no Mikoto (Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto = Isonotakeru?), identified as the wood (tree) deity Iitakeru (Itsu no Takeri). * Ōnamuchi no Mikoto (Ōkuninushi no Mikoto) In addition, Inari Jinja, Kakimoto-sha, and Tenjin-sha are enshrined in the same hall. The "Sōyuyama Engi (Sōyu-san Engi)" describes this shrine as the “jinushigami” (local guardian deity) of Izusan Jinja. Because “Kinomiya” can be interpreted as “I no Miya” meaning “忌の宮” (taboo shrine), many people come here to pray for abstinence from certain things (such as alcohol). == History == The founding time is unknown. According to shrine tradition, in Wadō 3 (710), fishermen found what seemed to be a divine wooden root caught in their fishing net three times in Atami Bay. They enshrined this root under a pine tree and offered roasted barley flour (mugi-kogashi). That night, Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto appeared in a dream, complaining about the noise of the sea, so they moved the deity to the current location in the forest. Because it was originally a wooden root, the shrine came to be called “Ki no Miya” (Kinomiya). This tradition strongly reflects “Kinomiya faith,” where driftwood or a piece of wood is worshiped, and Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto is revered as a wood (tree) deity. There is also a legend that Sakanoue no Tamuramaro prayed for victory here and enshrined divided spirits of this deity in various places in the Tohoku region. The shrine was a village shrine under the modern shrine system. After World War II, given its history and activities, it was added to the list of Beppyo Shrines under the Association of Shinto Shrines. [[File:Kinomiya jinja - March 7 2021 - various 14 58 24 831000.jpeg|thumb|Torii]] === Position in Atami City === Located in the hilly area near the center of the city, Kinomiya Jinja is considered a central shrine of the Atami area. Its festival, the Kogashi Matsuri (below), is Atami’s largest festival. It also performs rituals for many other shrines in Atami City that do not have their own resident priest. Only Izusan Jinja, Imamiya Jinja, and Ajiko Jinja have their own priests. Other shrines such as Misogino Taki Jinja, Meisui Jinja, Danna Jinja, Fujimori Inari Jinja, Yunomae Jinja, Goten Inari Jinja, Dairokuten-son Jinja, Tagajinja, Shimotaga Jinja, Tsushima Jinja, Koyama Shinmeigū, Wadanoki Jinja, and others are served by Kinomiya Jinja’s priests. Wada Hachiman Jinja’s rites are conducted by Imamiya Jinja’s priest, and Hatsuki Jinja on Hatsushima (an offshore island of Atami) is served by Izusan Jinja’s priest. As Atami’s tourism fortunes waned after the Bubble Economy collapse, pilgrimages to Kinomiya Jinja also declined. However, as Atami tourism recovered in the 2010s, Kinomiya Jinja also saw an increase in visitors. They introduced selfie stands, an open cafe, walking guides, and collaborated with local shops to create new sweets. In 2017, about 688,000 people visited, over four times the roughly 157,000 in 2008.[https://mainichi.jp/articles/20181203/dde/001/040/033000c “Check: Rebound with a Sacred Camphor Tree—Kinomiya Jinja in Atami leverages youth and female appeal”], Mainichi Shimbun (Evening edition), December 3, 2018, p.1. Accessed December 7, 2018. == Main festivals == === Kogashi Matsuri === * festival “Kogashi Matsuri” held around July 15 (including the eve on July 14 and events through July 16). Originally, as old lunar calendar June 15 was the day the fishermen discovered the wooden deity, they held the festival then, but in Meiji times it changed to the solar calendar.[http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/reitaisai.html festival] Kinomiya Jinja official site ** July 14: Eve festival (Yoi-miya-sai), praying for successful ceremonies. ** July 15: festival “Kogashi Matsuri” *** “Miya Mikoshi Togyo” (9:00–15:00): The shrine’s mikoshi visits Atami Station, Shinsui Park, Ginza-chō, and other city areas. *** “Reitaisai Hōhei” (11:00–): Offerings of mugikogashi (roasted barley flour), lily bulbs, bitter oranges, and tokoro jelly according to tradition. *** “Hōshuku Shinnei Gishiki” (11:40–13:00): Kashima Odori (Kashima dance), Miko Kagura (shrine maiden dance), Urayasu no Mai. *** “Kogashi Matsuri Dashi Contest” (18:30–21:30): About 30+ festival floats line up on National Route 135, which is closed off near Hotel Ōnoya through Atami Sun Beach, competing in a parade-style contest. ** July 16: *** “Jinkō-sai” (Shinkō-sai) **** “Hōshuku Shinnei Gishiki” (8:30–): Kashima Odori, Miko Kagura, Urayasu no Mai **** “Goshinkō Gyōretsu” (9:50–15:40): A procession of about 500 people including Tengu-masked, high-geta wearing Sarutahiko distributing mugikogashi (symbolizing rice), a Mikoshi, Shishimai (lion dance), priests, etc. They visit Yunomae Jinja, Atami Station, Sun Beach (with a mikoshi purification), Nagisa Kōen (with dances), and Ginza. At Ginza (in front of Ozawa Himono-ten[http://atamii.jp/today/73259/ Goshinkō parade in Atami city by Kinomiya Jinja concluding festival], Atami Net News, 2017/7/17), Kashima Odori is also performed. **** “Kanchōsai” (15:40–) *** “Kogashi Matsuri Dashi Contest” (18:30–21:00) === Setsubun festival === On Setsubun (February 3), a lively bean-throwing ceremony takes place with participating celebrities. Past participants include: * Izumi Pinko * Ehara Hiroyuki * Kuroda Arthur * Satō Yōko (violinist) * Nishikido Oyakata (former sumo wrestler Mitoizumi Masato) * Hashida Sugako * Hayashi Mariko * Motoki Daisuke == Shrine Buildings == The honden is nagare-zukuri style, connected with heiden and haiden in a gongen-zukuri arrangement. == Subsidiary Shrines == Within the precincts: * Kinomiya Inari-sha (Inari shrine from Fushimi Inari Taisha in Kyoto) * Kinomiya Benzaiten (Benzaiten statue by Takamura Kōun is shown on November 23) * Mitsumine Jinja [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/top/setsumassha.html Kinomiya Jinja – Subsidiary Shrines] (Accessed December 7, 2018) == Cultural Properties == [[File:Azusawake Jinja no Okusu -02.jpg|thumb|150px|Great Camphor Tree of Azusawake Jinja]] === National Natural Monument === {{Main|{{ill|Azusawake Jinja no Ōkusu|ja|阿豆佐和気神社の大クス}}|{{ill|Kamanariya Heishichi|ja|釜鳴屋平七}}}} * The Great Camphor Tree of Azusawake Jinja (over 2000 years old, trunk circumference about 24m, height 20m), designated in Shōwa 8. Circling it once is said to extend life by one year or grant wishes. Historically, seven camphor trees stood here, but during the Ansei era (1855–60), a dispute related to fishing rights (the Ōami/maguro-ami incident) forced them to cut five for lawsuit costs.[https://www.city.atami.lg.jp/kosodate/shogaigakushu/1011165/1006016/1009091/1009107.html Episode 14: Local Hero Kamanariya Heishichi] - Atami City Hall[http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/supporting_party/ 50th Anniversary of Iitakeru no Mikoto’s 1300th Enshrinement: Rebuilding Senshūden and Grounds Improvement Project] - Kinomiya Jinja Another large camphor stands near the entrance. === Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property === * Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori (Kashima dance) Performed during the Kogashi Matsuri at the shrine grounds, Atami Station front, Nagisa Kōen, and Ginza Street. The dancers carry ladles with colored papers symbolizing rice grains, praying for abundant harvest and warding off evil. It’s recognized as a Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property. {{citation needed|Kinomiya Jinja}} == Trees == Horuto-no-ki ([[Elaeocarpus sylvestris|Elaeacarpus sylvestris var. ellipticus]]): A unique evergreen species rare to Japan. Characterized by smooth gray bark and leathery leaves, it produces white flowers in July or August. Its leaves turn red before shedding. Two species of this genus grow wild in the warm temperate regions of Japan. Kinomiya no O-kusu (Camphor Tree, Cinnamomum camphora): This colossal tree, standing 23 meters in circumference and estimated to be over 2,000 years old, is recognized as Japan's second largest and oldest kusunoki tree. Known as Goshinboku, or the Holy Tree, it's believed that a Shinto god resides within it. Many believe the tree possesses special powers, granting health, safety, and longevity to those who visit. The bark of this tree is brown and lightly fissured, and its wood is often used in furniture and sculpture. Extracts from the leaves of this tree have medicinal uses in Chinese medicine. It is designated as a natural monument. == Other natural treasures == Beyond the Kinomiya Shrine, other notable trees include Japan's largest camphor tree located at a Hachiman Shrine in Kamo-cho, Kagoshima, and the oldest tree in Japan, a 3,000-year-old kusunoki found in Saga Prefecture. The Kinomiya Shrine is surrounded by a woodland which can be classified as a small laurel forest or ''shoyo-juinrin''. Many trees in this forest are broadleaf evergreens, safeguarding aspects of the local flora from development. == Other == * In May 2011, a 300-year-old holly oak tree next to the torii toppled at its base and damaged the 1920s torii. == Access == * About a 5-minute walk from [[Kinomiya Station]] (JR Itō Line). Also walkable (about 18 minutes) from [[Atami Station]] or reachable by city bus (Ten Nation Pass line or Nishiyama loop) to “Kinomiya Jinja Mae” bus stop.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/praying/access/|title=Access|publisher=Kinomiya Jinja|accessdate=2021-04-21}} The shrine grounds are open from 9:00 to 17:00. == References == * Tanigawa Ken’ichi ed., "Nihon no Kami, Jinja to Seichi Vol.10 Tōkai", Hakusuisha, 1987 == See Also == * Kinomiya faith * Kashima Odori == Notes == === Notes === {{notelist}} === Sources === {{Reflist|2}} == External Links == {{commonscat|Kinomiya-jinja}} * [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/ Official Website of Kinomiya Jinja] * [https://atami.travel/atami-tourism/kinomiya-shrin/ Atami Tourism Bureau - Kinomiya Jinja] * {{Cultural Heritage Online|22_shizuoka|7274|Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property: Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori}} {{Shinto Navbox}} {{Shinto-stub}} {{citation needed|Kinomiya Jinja}} {{Draft categories| }} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{Source Wikipedia}} {{draft categories| }} {{draft categories| [[Category:Shinto shrines in Shizuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:History of Atami]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Atami]] [[Category:Yamato Takeru]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:beppyo shrines without templates]] [[Category:Son-sha]] [[Category:Kinomo]] [[Category:Atami, Shizuoka]] [[Category:cCompletion tier 2]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[Category:r]] [[Category:11]] [[Category:Pages from everybodywiki under right title]] [[Category:New]] }} [[sn:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[en:draft:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[en:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[ja:%E6%9D%A5%E5%AE%AE%E7%A5%9E%E7%A4%BE]] [[Category:Ja import oversized]]

In 2017, about 688,000 people visited, over four times the roughly 157,000 in 2008.[https://mainichi.jp/articles/20181203/dde/001/040/033000c “Check: Rebound with a Sacred Camphor Tree—Kinomiya Jinja in Atami leverages youth and female appeal”], Mainichi Shimbun (Evening edition), December 3, 2018, p.1. Accessed December 7, 2018. == Main festivals == === Kogashi Matsuri === * festival “Kogashi Matsuri” held around July 15 (including the eve on July 14 and events through July 16). Originally, as old lunar calendar June 15 was the day the fishermen discovered the wooden deity, they held the festival then, but in Meiji times it changed to the solar calendar.[http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/reitaisai.html festival] Kinomiya Jinja official site ** July 14: Eve festival (Yoi-miya-sai), praying for successful ceremonies. ** July 15: festival “Kogashi Matsuri” *** “Miya Mikoshi Togyo” (9:00–15:00): The shrine’s mikoshi visits Atami Station, Shinsui Park, Ginza-chō, and other city areas. *** “Reitaisai Hōhei” (11:00–): Offerings of mugikogashi (roasted barley flour), lily bulbs, bitter oranges, and tokoro jelly according to tradition. *** “Hōshuku Shinnei Gishiki” (11:40–13:00): Kashima Odori (Kashima dance), Miko Kagura (shrine maiden dance), Urayasu no Mai. *** “Kogashi Matsuri Dashi Contest” (18:30–21:30): About 30+ festival floats line up on National Route 135, which is closed off near Hotel Ōnoya through Atami Sun Beach, competing in a parade-style contest. ** July 16: *** “Jinkō-sai” (Shinkō-sai) **** “Hōshuku Shinnei Gishiki” (8:30–): Kashima Odori, Miko Kagura, Urayasu no Mai **** “Goshinkō Gyōretsu” (9:50–15:40): A procession of about 500 people including Tengu-masked, high-geta wearing Sarutahiko distributing mugikogashi (symbolizing rice), a Mikoshi, Shishimai (lion dance), priests, etc. They visit Yunomae Jinja, Atami Station, Sun Beach (with a mikoshi purification), Nagisa Kōen (with dances), and Ginza. At Ginza (in front of Ozawa Himono-ten[http://atamii.jp/today/73259/ Goshinkō parade in Atami city by Kinomiya Jinja concluding festival], Atami Net News, 2017/7/17), Kashima Odori is also performed. **** “Kanchōsai” (15:40–) *** “Kogashi Matsuri Dashi Contest” (18:30–21:00) === Setsubun festival === On Setsubun (February 3), a lively bean-throwing ceremony takes place with participating celebrities. Past participants include: * Izumi Pinko * Ehara Hiroyuki * Kuroda Arthur * Satō Yōko (violinist) * Nishikido Oyakata (former sumo wrestler Mitoizumi Masato) * Hashida Sugako * Hayashi Mariko * Motoki Daisuke == Shrine Buildings == The honden is nagare-zukuri style, connected with heiden and haiden in a gongen-zukuri arrangement. == Subsidiary Shrines == Within the precincts: * Kinomiya Inari-sha (Inari shrine from Fushimi Inari Taisha in Kyoto) * Kinomiya Benzaiten (Benzaiten statue by Takamura Kōun is shown on November 23) * Mitsumine Jinja [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/top/setsumassha.html Kinomiya Jinja – Subsidiary Shrines] (Accessed December 7, 2018) == Cultural Properties == [[File:Azusawake Jinja no Okusu -02.jpg|thumb|150px|Great Camphor Tree of Azusawake Jinja]] === National Natural Monument === {{Main|{{ill|Azusawake Jinja no Ōkusu|ja|阿豆佐和気神社の大クス}}|{{ill|Kamanariya Heishichi|ja|釜鳴屋平七}}}} * The Great Camphor Tree of Azusawake Jinja (over 2000 years old, trunk circumference about 24m, height 20m), designated in Shōwa 8. Circling it once is said to extend life by one year or grant wishes. Historically, seven camphor trees stood here, but during the Ansei era (1855–60), a dispute related to fishing rights (the Ōami/maguro-ami incident) forced them to cut five for lawsuit costs.[https://www.city.atami.lg.jp/kosodate/shogaigakushu/1011165/1006016/1009091/1009107.html Episode 14: Local Hero Kamanariya Heishichi] - Atami City Hall[http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/supporting_party/ 50th Anniversary of Iitakeru no Mikoto’s 1300th Enshrinement: Rebuilding Senshūden and Grounds Improvement Project] - Kinomiya Jinja Another large camphor stands near the entrance. === Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property === * Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori (Kashima dance) Performed during the Kogashi Matsuri at the shrine grounds, Atami Station front, Nagisa Kōen, and Ginza Street. The dancers carry ladles with colored papers symbolizing rice grains, praying for abundant harvest and warding off evil. It’s recognized as a Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property. {{citation needed|Kinomiya Jinja}} == Trees == Horuto-no-ki ([[Elaeocarpus sylvestris|Elaeacarpus sylvestris var. ellipticus]]): A unique evergreen species rare to Japan. Characterized by smooth gray bark and leathery leaves, it produces white flowers in July or August. Its leaves turn red before shedding. Two species of this genus grow wild in the warm temperate regions of Japan. Kinomiya no O-kusu (Camphor Tree, Cinnamomum camphora): This colossal tree, standing 23 meters in circumference and estimated to be over 2,000 years old, is recognized as Japan's second largest and oldest kusunoki tree. Known as Goshinboku, or the Holy Tree, it's believed that a Shinto god resides within it. Many believe the tree possesses special powers, granting health, safety, and longevity to those who visit. The bark of this tree is brown and lightly fissured, and its wood is often used in furniture and sculpture. Extracts from the leaves of this tree have medicinal uses in Chinese medicine. It is designated as a natural monument. == Other natural treasures == Beyond the Kinomiya Shrine, other notable trees include Japan's largest camphor tree located at a Hachiman Shrine in Kamo-cho, Kagoshima, and the oldest tree in Japan, a 3,000-year-old kusunoki found in Saga Prefecture. The Kinomiya Shrine is surrounded by a woodland which can be classified as a small laurel forest or ''shoyo-juinrin''. Many trees in this forest are broadleaf evergreens, safeguarding aspects of the local flora from development. == Other == * In May 2011, a 300-year-old holly oak tree next to the torii toppled at its base and damaged the 1920s torii. == Access == * About a 5-minute walk from [[Kinomiya Station]] (JR Itō Line). Also walkable (about 18 minutes) from [[Atami Station]] or reachable by city bus (Ten Nation Pass line or Nishiyama loop) to “Kinomiya Jinja Mae” bus stop.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/praying/access/|title=Access|publisher=Kinomiya Jinja|accessdate=2021-04-21}} The shrine grounds are open from 9:00 to 17:00. == References == * Tanigawa Ken’ichi ed., "Nihon no Kami, Jinja to Seichi Vol.10 Tōkai", Hakusuisha, 1987 == See Also == * Kinomiya faith * Kashima Odori == Notes == === Notes === {{notelist}} === Sources === {{Reflist|2}} == External Links == {{commonscat|Kinomiya-jinja}} * [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/ Official Website of Kinomiya Jinja] * [https://atami.travel/atami-tourism/kinomiya-shrin/ Atami Tourism Bureau - Kinomiya Jinja] * {{Cultural Heritage Online|22_shizuoka|7274|Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property: Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori}} {{Shinto Navbox}} {{Shinto-stub}} {{citation needed|Kinomiya Jinja}} {{Draft categories| }} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{Source Wikipedia}} {{draft categories| }} {{draft categories| [[Category:Shinto shrines in Shizuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:History of Atami]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Atami]] [[Category:Yamato Takeru]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:beppyo shrines without templates]] [[Category:Son-sha]] [[Category:Kinomo]] [[Category:Atami, Shizuoka]] [[Category:cCompletion tier 2]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[Category:r]] [[Category:11]] [[Category:Pages from everybodywiki under right title]] [[Category:New]] }} [[sn:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[en:draft:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[en:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[ja:%E6%9D%A5%E5%AE%AE%E7%A5%9E%E7%A4%BE]]

{{Otheruses|[[静岡県]][[熱海市]]の神社|静岡県[[伊豆市]]八幡の神社|来宮神社 (伊豆市八幡)|静岡県[[賀茂郡]][[東伊豆町]]白田の神社|志理太乎宜神社}} {{神社 |名称 = 来宮神社 |画像 = [[File:Kinomiya Shrine Haiden.jpg|250px]]
拝殿
{{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|marker=religious-shinto|zoom=13|frame-align=center|frame-width=250}} |所在地 = [[静岡県]][[熱海市]]西山町43-1 |位置 = {{coord|35|06|01.8|N|139|04|04.1|E|region:JP-22_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} |祭神 = [[ヤマトタケル|日本武尊]]
[[五十猛神|五十猛命]]
[[大国主|大己貴命]] |社格 = 旧[[村社]]
[[別表神社]] |創建 = （伝）[[和銅]]3年（[[710年]]） |本殿 = [[流造]] |例祭 = [[7月15日]] |神事 = こがし祭（7月15・16日） }} [[File:Cinnamomum camphora 20100612 (Kinomiya Shrine) (B).jpg|thumb|阿豆佐和気神社の大クス]] [[File:Cinnamomum camphora 20100612 (Kinomiya Shrine) (2nd).jpg|thumb|第2大クス]] '''来宮神社'''（きのみやじんじゃ）は、[[静岡県]][[熱海市]]にある[[神社]]である。[[近代社格制度|社格]]は[[村社|旧村社]]。 == 社名 == 古くは「木宮明神」や「来宮大明神」などと呼ばれた。[[明治維新]]後、[[式内社]]「阿豆佐和気命神社」に比定されたため、「阿豆佐和気神社」（あずさわけじんじゃ）を称したが、その非が判り現社名に復称した{{efn|ただし、社において配布されている小冊子には現在でも「[[延喜式神名帳]]には『阿豆佐別神社』アズサワケジンジャの名で記されております」とある。}}{{efn|式内 阿豆佐和氣命神社の論社には、他に[[東京都]][[利島村]]の「阿豆佐和気命神社」がある{{Cite web|和書|url=http://www.tokyo-jinjacho.or.jp/tosho/2843/|title=阿豆佐和気命神社|publisher=東京都神社庁|accessdate=2021-04-21}}。}}。 == 祭神 == *[[ヤマトタケル|日本武尊]] *[[五十猛神|五十猛命]]（いたけるのみこと） *[[大国主|大己貴命]]（おおなもちのみこと） 上記3柱を主祭神として、稲荷神社・柿本社・天神社を[[相殿]]に祀る。『[[走湯山縁起]]』は[[伊豆山神社]]の[[地主神]]としている。 「きのみや」を「忌の宮」と解し、禁酒など[[断ち物]]の祈願をする者も多い。 == 歴史 == 創建時期は定かではないが、社伝によると[[和銅]]3年（[[710年]]）、[[熱海湾]]で網に木の根が掛かる事が3度重なり、不思議に思った漁師があらためると[[神像]]のようであったので、近くの[[マツ|松]]の下に祀って、持っていた[[はったい粉|麦こがし]]を供えた。その夜の夢に五十猛命が現れ、潮騒が耳障りであるとの神託があり、現在地に遷祀したといい、木の根を[[神体]]としたところから「木の宮」と称えたという。漂着物を祀ったのに始まり、祭神を木の神'''五十猛命'''とするなど、[[キノミヤ信仰]]が顕著に認められる神社である。なお、[[坂上田村麻呂]]が戦勝を祈願し、当社の分霊を東北地方を始め各地に鎮座させたという伝承もある。 旧社格は村社であったが、[[戦後]]その歴史や活動状況に鑑み、[[神社本庁]]の[[別表神社]]に加えられた。 [[ファイル:Kinomiya jinja - March 7 2021 - various 14 58 24 831000.jpeg|thumb|鳥居]] === 熱海市内における位置付け === 熱海市街地中心部の山の手にある神社ということで、来宮神社は熱海市内全体においても中心的な神社として扱われている。そしてその[[例大祭]]である「こがし祭」（下述）は、市内最大の祭りとして大々的に催されている。 また、独自の[[宮司]]を擁する伊豆山地区の[[伊豆山神社]]、市街地南部の[[今宮神社 (熱海市)|今宮神社]]、網代地区の[[阿治古神社]]以外の市内の神社、具体的には、 *みそぎの滝神社（糸川上流、緑ガ丘町） *明水神社（糸川上流、西山町） *丹那神社（[[丹那トンネル]]入り口上） *藤森稲荷神社（市街地・咲見町） *[[湯前神社]]（市街地・上宿町） *御殿稲荷神社（市街地・中央町） *大六天尊神社（市街地・東海岸町） *[[多賀神社 (熱海市)|多賀神社]]（多賀地区北部・上多賀） *[[下多賀神社]]（多賀地区南部・下多賀） *津島神社（多賀地区南部・下多賀（中野）） *小山神明宮（多賀地区南部・下多賀（小山）） *[[和田木神社]]（多賀地区南部・下多賀（和田木）） などの神社の神事・祭祀は、来宮神社の宮司によって執り行われている。（和田町にある和田八幡神社の神事は、近隣の今宮神社の宮司が行い、伊豆山神社の[[境外社]]で、熱海沖の[[初島]]にある[[初木神社]]の神事・祭祀は、伊豆山神社の宮司によって執り行われている。） 観光地としての熱海とも人気が連動しており、[[熱海温泉]]が低迷した[[バブル崩壊]]後は、来宮神社への参拝者も減少した。熱海観光の人気が復活した2010年代には、来宮神社も[[自分撮り|自撮り]]や[[インスタグラム]]用の写真撮影がしやすい台やオープンカフェ、散策案内所の設置、周辺商店との連携による[[スイーツ]]開発などに取り組んだ。2017年度の参拝者は約68万8000人で、2008年度（約15万7000人）の4倍以上に増えた[https://mainichi.jp/articles/20181203/dde/001/040/033000c 【チェック】「映える」ご神木で復活／熱海・来宮神社／若者・女性を意識 境内にカフェも]『毎日新聞』夕刊2018年12月3日（1面）2018年12月7日閲覧。。 == 主な神事 == === こがし祭 === *[[例祭]]「'''こがし祭'''」（[[7月15日]]を中心に、前日の[[宵宮祭]]も含めて7月14日〜7月16日の3日間 [http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/reitaisai.html 例大祭] 来宮神社公式サイト。御木像である木の根を漁民が拾ったのが[[旧暦]]6月15日であったので、この日に祭典を行っていたが、[[明治]]以降[[新暦]]に改めた。） **7月14日 - '''宵宮祭'''（よいみやさい）。神事が無事終わるよう祈念。 **7月15日 - 例大祭「こがし祭」 ***'''宮[[神輿]]渡御'''（9:00〜15:00） - 神輿で[[熱海駅]]、[[親水公園 (熱海市)|親水公園]]、銀座町など市街地を巡る。 ***'''例大祭[[奉幣]]'''（11:00～） - 創建時の伝承に因んで、'''[[麦こがし]]'''を中心に[[ユリ根|百合根]]、[[ダイダイ|橙]]、[[ところてん|ところ]]を供える。 ***'''奉祝神賑行事'''（11:40～13:00） - [[鹿島踊]]（かしまおどり）、[[神女神楽]]（みこかぐら）、[[浦安の舞]]（うらやすのまい） ***'''[[こがし祭り山車コンクール]]'''（18:30〜21:30） - [[ホテル大野屋]]前から[[熱海サンビーチ]]前までの[[国道135号]]を通行止めにし、市街地各町内の30以上の[[山車]]（だし）が集まってコンクールを兼ねたパレードが行われる。 **7月16日 ***'''[[神幸祭]]'''（じんこうさい） ****'''奉祝神賑行事'''（8:30～） - 鹿島踊、神女神楽、浦安の舞 ****'''御[[神幸]]行列'''（9:50〜15:40） - 先導役の[[天狗]]面・[[高下駄]]で御利益ある[[麦こがし]]を撒く[[サルタヒコ|猿田彦神]]、「みょうねん（妙念）」を掛け声とする御[[鳳輦]]、[[獅子舞]]、その他宮司・[[神官]]・総代などを含む総勢500名の御神幸行列が、[[湯前神社]]、熱海駅、サンビーチ、渚小公園、清水町、銀座、市役所などを巡る。
湯前神社・熱海駅・[[熱海銀座商店街|銀座通り]]（小沢ひもの店前[http://atamii.jp/today/73259/ 【来宮神社】御神幸行列が熱海市街を巡行　例大祭が閉幕] 熱海ネット新聞 2017/7/17）では鹿島踊が、サンビーチでは御鳳輦の浜降り神事が、[[渚小公園]]では奉祝神賑行事（鹿島踊・神女神楽・浦安の舞）が、それぞれ執り行われる。 ****'''還幸祭'''（15:40〜） ***'''こがし祭り山車コンクール'''（18:30〜21:00） === 節分祭 === [[節分]]（2月3日）の夕方に芸能人・著名人も参加して、賑やかに豆撒きが行われる。過去参加した主な芸能人・著名人は以下の通り。（50音順） * [[泉ピン子]] * [[江原啓之]] * [[黒田アーサー]] * [[佐藤陽子 (ヴァイオリニスト)|佐藤陽子]] * [[錦戸親方]]（元・[[水戸泉政人|水戸泉]]） * [[橋田壽賀子]] * [[林真理子]] * [[元木大介]] == 社殿 == [[本殿]]は[[流造]]。[[幣殿]]、[[拝殿]]を連結する[[権現造]]となっている。 == 境内社 == [[境内]]には[[摂末社]]として、 * [[稲荷神社|来宮稲荷社]]（京都の[[伏見稲荷大社]]より勧請） * [[弁才天|来宮弁財天]]（11月23日に[[開帳]]される弁財天像は[[高村光雲]]作） * [[三峯神社]] の三社がある[http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/top/setsumassha.html 來宮神社 摂末社]（2018年12月7日閲覧）。。 == 文化財 == [[ファイル:Azusawake Jinja no Okusu -02.jpg|thumb|150px|阿豆佐和気神社の大クス]] === 天然記念物（国指定） === {{関連記事|阿豆佐和気神社の大クス|釜鳴屋平七}} *阿豆佐和気神社の大クス（あずさわけじんじゃのおおくす） :本殿裏にあり、推定[[樹齢]]2000年以上、一部枯れているが樹高約20m、幹周り約24mの[[クスノキ|大楠]]で、[[昭和]]8年に[[天然記念物]]に指定された。これを1周すると寿命が1年延びるとか、願い事が叶うなどと信仰されている。以前は境内に7株の大楠があったが、[[安政]]年間（1855〜60年）の頃、'''大網事件/鮪網事件'''という漁業権を巡る争議が起こり、訴訟費等捻出のために5株を伐採した（参考: [[釜鳴屋平七]]）[https://www.city.atami.lg.jp/kosodate/shogaigakushu/1011165/1006016/1009091/1009107.html 第14話「郷土の義人 釜鳴屋平七」] - 熱海市役所[http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/supporting_party/ 御祭神五十猛命御鎮座1300年記念事業 参集殿建設及び境内整備事業趣意書] - 来宮神社。旧記によると、この木も伐ろうとしたところ、白髪の老翁が現れて立ち塞がり、樵夫の持つ大鋸を2つに折ってどこかへ消えたので、それ以来[[神木]]として崇めるようになったという。もう1株も神社の入口付近に残存し第2大楠と呼ばれている。なお、天然記念物指定名称に「阿豆佐和気神社」と冠せられているのは、それが指定当時の社名であったためである。 === 静岡県指定無形民俗文化財 === *来宮神社 [[鹿島踊]]（かしまおどり） :'''こがし祭'''において、境内、[[熱海駅]]前、渚小公園、銀座通りにある木像を拾った漁師の子孫と伝える家の前（小沢ひもの店前）で奉納され、古式をよく伝えるものとして[[静岡県指定文化財一覧|静岡県指定無形民俗文化財]]に指定されている。踊り手は来宮神社鹿島踊保存会の男性30名程度で構成され、[[色紙]]を入れた[[柄杓]]を持つ。柄杓からこぼれ落ちた色紙は[[コメ|稲米]]を表し、五穀豊穣・[[厄祓い|厄払い]]の意味を持つという。 == その他 == *2011年5月、[[鳥居]]脇の[[ホルトノキ]]（樹齢約300年）が根元から倒壊して鳥居（1920年建立）を直撃、破損した。[http://www.yomiuri.co.jp/e-japan/shizuoka/news/20110503-OYT8T00538.htm] == 交通 == *[[東日本旅客鉄道|JR]][[伊東線]][[来宮駅]]より徒歩5分程度。JR[[熱海駅]]からも徒歩圏内（18分程度）で、[[路線バス]]もある（十国峠行または西山循環で「来宮神社前」[[バス停留所|停留所]]下車）{{Cite web|和書|url=http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/praying/access/ |title=アクセス・交通 |publisher=熱海 來宮神社 |accessdate=2021-04-21}}。なお、神社の開頭時間は9時から17時となっている。 == 参考文献 == *[[谷川健一]]編 『日本の神々 神社と聖地』第10巻東海 [[白水社]]、1987年 ==関連項目== *[[キノミヤ信仰]] *[[鹿島踊]] ==脚注== {{脚注ヘルプ|2}} ===注釈=== {{notelist}} ===出典=== {{Reflist|2}} == 外部リンク == {{commonscat|Kinomiya-jinja}} *[http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/ 来宮神社 公式サイト] *[https://atami.travel/atami-tourism/kinomiya-shrin/ 熱海観光局-來宮神社] *{{地域文化資産ポータル|22_shizuoka|7274|静岡県指定無形民俗文化財 「来宮神社鹿島踊」}} {{神道 横}} {{shinto-stub}} {{DEFAULTSORT:きのみやしんしや}} [[Category:静岡県の神社]] [[Category:静岡県の旧村社]] [[Category:別表神社]] [[Category:熱海市の歴史]] [[Category:熱海市の建築物]] [[Category:ヤマトタケル]]

{{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=13|frame-align=center|frame-width=250}} | caption = | map_type = Japan Shizuoka | coordinates = {{coord|35|06|01.8|N|139|04|04.1|E|region:JP-22_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | location = 43-1 Nishiyamachō, {{ill|Atami, Shizuoka|ja|熱海市|lt=Atami City}}, {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|ja|静岡県|lt=Shizuoka Prefecture}} | deity = {{ubl|Yamato Takeru no Mikoto|Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto (Iitakeru no Mikoto)|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto (Ōkuninushi no Mikoto)}} | type = Former village shrine, Beppyo Shrine | founded = (Trad.) Wadō 3 (710) | honden = Nagare-zukuri style | festival = July 15 | ceremonies = Kogashi Matsuri (July 15–16) }} The [[Kinomiya Shrine]] is located in [[Atami]], [[Shizuoka (city)|Shizuoka]], and is famous for its natural treasures, especially the historic trees within its grounds.{{Cite web |last=Author |first=No |date=1999-12-08 |title=The natural treasures of Kinomiya Shrine |url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/1999/12/08/environment/the-natural-treasures-of-kinomiya-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-19 |website=The Japan Times |language=en}} It is located near [[Kinomiya Station]],{{Cite web |title=Expand your life expectancy at Kinomiya shrine, in Atami city｜TOMO – 供TOMO 玄米コーヒーオンラインストア |url=https://tomo.life/en/blogs/shinto-and-shrines/lets-visit-kinomiya-shrine |access-date=2023-10-19 |website=tomo.life}} and serves [[Amazake]]. [[File:Cinnamomum camphora 20100612 (Kinomiya Shrine) (B).jpg|thumb|The large camphor tree of Azusawake Jinja]] [[File:Cinnamomum camphora 20100612 (Kinomiya Shrine) (2nd).jpg|thumb|The second large camphor tree]] '''Kinomiya Jinja''' is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Atami|ja|熱海市|lt=Atami City}}, {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|ja|静岡県|lt=Shizuoka Prefecture}}, Japan. Under the modern shrine Rank system, it was once a village shrine. == Shrine name == Historically known as “Kimiya Myōjin” or “Kinomiya Daimyōjin,” among others. After the Meiji Restoration, it was identified as the “Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja” (阿豆佐和気命神社) as a result of being associated with a Shikinaisha of that name. Later, when it was found that this was incorrect, it reverted to its current name.{{efn|However, pamphlets distributed by the shrine still state, “It is recorded in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō as ‘Azusawake Jinja.’”}} {{efn|Other candidates for Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja include a shrine of the same name in Toshima Village, Tokyo.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=http://www.tokyo-jinjacho.or.jp/tosho/2843/|title=Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja|publisher=Tokyo Jinja-chō|accessdate=2021-04-21}}}} == Enshrined Deities == * Yamato Takeru no Mikoto * Iitakeru no Mikoto (Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto = Isonotakeru?), identified as the wood (tree) deity Iitakeru (Itsu no Takeri). * Ōnamuchi no Mikoto (Ōkuninushi no Mikoto) In addition, Inari Jinja, Kakimoto-sha, and Tenjin-sha are enshrined in the same hall. The "Sōyuyama Engi (Sōyu-san Engi)" describes this shrine as the “jinushigami” (local guardian deity) of Izusan Jinja. Because “Kinomiya” can be interpreted as “I no Miya” meaning “忌の宮” (taboo shrine), many people come here to pray for abstinence from certain things (such as alcohol). == History == The founding time is unknown. According to shrine tradition, in Wadō 3 (710), fishermen found what seemed to be a divine wooden root caught in their fishing net three times in Atami Bay. They enshrined this root under a pine tree and offered roasted barley flour (mugi-kogashi). That night, Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto appeared in a dream, complaining about the noise of the sea, so they moved the deity to the current location in the forest. Because it was originally a wooden root, the shrine came to be called “Ki no Miya” (Kinomiya). This tradition strongly reflects “Kinomiya faith,” where driftwood or a piece of wood is worshiped, and Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto is revered as a wood (tree) deity. There is also a legend that Sakanoue no Tamuramaro prayed for victory here and enshrined divided spirits of this deity in various places in the Tohoku region. The shrine was a village shrine under the modern shrine system. After World War II, given its history and activities, it was added to the list of Beppyo Shrines under the Association of Shinto Shrines. [[File:Kinomiya jinja - March 7 2021 - various 14 58 24 831000.jpeg|thumb|Torii]] === Position in Atami City === Located in the hilly area near the center of the city, Kinomiya Jinja is considered a central shrine of the Atami area. Its festival, the Kogashi Matsuri (below), is Atami’s largest festival. It also performs rituals for many other shrines in Atami City that do not have their own resident priest. Only Izusan Jinja, Imamiya Jinja, and Ajiko Jinja have their own priests. Other shrines such as Misogino Taki Jinja, Meisui Jinja, Danna Jinja, Fujimori Inari Jinja, Yunomae Jinja, Goten Inari Jinja, Dairokuten-son Jinja, Tagajinja, Shimotaga Jinja, Tsushima Jinja, Koyama Shinmeigū, Wadanoki Jinja, and others are served by Kinomiya Jinja’s priests. Wada Hachiman Jinja’s rites are conducted by Imamiya Jinja’s priest, and Hatsuki Jinja on Hatsushima (an offshore island of Atami) is served by Izusan Jinja’s priest. As Atami’s tourism fortunes waned after the Bubble Economy collapse, pilgrimages to Kinomiya Jinja also declined. However, as Atami tourism recovered in the 2010s, Kinomiya Jinja also saw an increase in visitors. They introduced selfie stands, an open cafe, walking guides, and collaborated with local shops to create new sweets. In 2017, about 688,000 people visited, over four times the roughly 157,000 in 2008.[https://mainichi.jp/articles/20181203/dde/001/040/033000c “Check: Rebound with a Sacred Camphor Tree—Kinomiya Jinja in Atami leverages youth and female appeal”], Mainichi Shimbun (Evening edition), December 3, 2018, p.1. Accessed December 7, 2018. == Main festivals == === Kogashi Matsuri === * festival “Kogashi Matsuri” held around July 15 (including the eve on July 14 and events through July 16). Originally, as old lunar calendar June 15 was the day the fishermen discovered the wooden deity, they held the festival then, but in Meiji times it changed to the solar calendar.[http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/reitaisai.html festival] Kinomiya Jinja official site ** July 14: Eve festival (Yoi-miya-sai), praying for successful ceremonies. ** July 15: festival “Kogashi Matsuri” *** “Miya Mikoshi Togyo” (9:00–15:00): The shrine’s mikoshi visits Atami Station, Shinsui Park, Ginza-chō, and other city areas. *** “Reitaisai Hōhei” (11:00–): Offerings of mugikogashi (roasted barley flour), lily bulbs, bitter oranges, and tokoro jelly according to tradition. *** “Hōshuku Shinnei Gishiki” (11:40–13:00): Kashima Odori (Kashima dance), Miko Kagura (shrine maiden dance), Urayasu no Mai. *** “Kogashi Matsuri Dashi Contest” (18:30–21:30): About 30+ festival floats line up on National Route 135, which is closed off near Hotel Ōnoya through Atami Sun Beach, competing in a parade-style contest. ** July 16: *** “Jinkō-sai” (Shinkō-sai) **** “Hōshuku Shinnei Gishiki” (8:30–): Kashima Odori, Miko Kagura, Urayasu no Mai **** “Goshinkō Gyōretsu” (9:50–15:40): A procession of about 500 people including Tengu-masked, high-geta wearing Sarutahiko distributing mugikogashi (symbolizing rice), a Mikoshi, Shishimai (lion dance), priests, etc. They visit Yunomae Jinja, Atami Station, Sun Beach (with a mikoshi purification), Nagisa Kōen (with dances), and Ginza. At Ginza (in front of Ozawa Himono-ten[http://atamii.jp/today/73259/ Goshinkō parade in Atami city by Kinomiya Jinja concluding festival], Atami Net News, 2017/7/17), Kashima Odori is also performed. **** “Kanchōsai” (15:40–) *** “Kogashi Matsuri Dashi Contest” (18:30–21:00) === Setsubun festival === On Setsubun (February 3), a lively bean-throwing ceremony takes place with participating celebrities. Past participants include: * Izumi Pinko * Ehara Hiroyuki * Kuroda Arthur * Satō Yōko (violinist) * Nishikido Oyakata (former sumo wrestler Mitoizumi Masato) * Hashida Sugako * Hayashi Mariko * Motoki Daisuke == Shrine Buildings == The honden is nagare-zukuri style, connected with heiden and haiden in a gongen-zukuri arrangement. == Subsidiary Shrines == Within the precincts: * Kinomiya Inari-sha (Inari shrine from Fushimi Inari Taisha in Kyoto) * Kinomiya Benzaiten (Benzaiten statue by Takamura Kōun is shown on November 23) * Mitsumine Jinja [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/top/setsumassha.html Kinomiya Jinja – Subsidiary Shrines] (Accessed December 7, 2018) == Cultural Properties == [[File:Azusawake Jinja no Okusu -02.jpg|thumb|150px|Great Camphor Tree of Azusawake Jinja]] === National Natural Monument === {{Main|{{ill|Azusawake Jinja no Ōkusu|ja|阿豆佐和気神社の大クス}}|{{ill|Kamanariya Heishichi|ja|釜鳴屋平七}}}} * The Great Camphor Tree of Azusawake Jinja (over 2000 years old, trunk circumference about 24m, height 20m), designated in Shōwa 8. Circling it once is said to extend life by one year or grant wishes. Historically, seven camphor trees stood here, but during the Ansei era (1855–60), a dispute related to fishing rights (the Ōami/maguro-ami incident) forced them to cut five for lawsuit costs.[https://www.city.atami.lg.jp/kosodate/shogaigakushu/1011165/1006016/1009091/1009107.html Episode 14: Local Hero Kamanariya Heishichi] - Atami City Hall[http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/supporting_party/ 50th Anniversary of Iitakeru no Mikoto’s 1300th Enshrinement: Rebuilding Senshūden and Grounds Improvement Project] - Kinomiya Jinja Another large camphor stands near the entrance. === Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property === * Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori (Kashima dance) Performed during the Kogashi Matsuri at the shrine grounds, Atami Station front, Nagisa Kōen, and Ginza Street. The dancers carry ladles with colored papers symbolizing rice grains, praying for abundant harvest and warding off evil. It’s recognized as a Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property. {{citation needed|Kinomiya Jinja}} == Trees == Horuto-no-ki ([[Elaeocarpus sylvestris|Elaeacarpus sylvestris var. ellipticus]]): A unique evergreen species rare to Japan. Characterized by smooth gray bark and leathery leaves, it produces white flowers in July or August. Its leaves turn red before shedding. Two species of this genus grow wild in the warm temperate regions of Japan. Kinomiya no O-kusu (Camphor Tree, Cinnamomum camphora): This colossal tree, standing 23 meters in circumference and estimated to be over 2,000 years old, is recognized as Japan's second largest and oldest kusunoki tree. Known as Goshinboku, or the Holy Tree, it's believed that a Shinto god resides within it. Many believe the tree possesses special powers, granting health, safety, and longevity to those who visit. The bark of this tree is brown and lightly fissured, and its wood is often used in furniture and sculpture. Extracts from the leaves of this tree have medicinal uses in Chinese medicine. It is designated as a natural monument. == Other natural treasures == Beyond the Kinomiya Shrine, other notable trees include Japan's largest camphor tree located at a Hachiman Shrine in Kamo-cho, Kagoshima, and the oldest tree in Japan, a 3,000-year-old kusunoki found in Saga Prefecture. The Kinomiya Shrine is surrounded by a woodland which can be classified as a small laurel forest or ''shoyo-juinrin''. Many trees in this forest are broadleaf evergreens, safeguarding aspects of the local flora from development. == Other == * In May 2011, a 300-year-old holly oak tree next to the torii toppled at its base and damaged the 1920s torii. == Access == * About a 5-minute walk from [[Kinomiya Station]] (JR Itō Line). Also walkable (about 18 minutes) from [[Atami Station]] or reachable by city bus (Ten Nation Pass line or Nishiyama loop) to “Kinomiya Jinja Mae” bus stop.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/praying/access/|title=Access|publisher=Kinomiya Jinja|accessdate=2021-04-21}} The shrine grounds are open from 9:00 to 17:00. == References == * Tanigawa Ken’ichi ed., "Nihon no Kami, Jinja to Seichi Vol.10 Tōkai", Hakusuisha, 1987 == See Also == * Kinomiya faith * Kashima Odori == Notes == === Notes === {{notelist}} === Sources === {{Reflist|2}} == External Links == {{commonscat|Kinomiya-jinja}} * [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/ Official Website of Kinomiya Jinja] * [https://atami.travel/atami-tourism/kinomiya-shrin/ Atami Tourism Bureau - Kinomiya Jinja] * {{Cultural Heritage Online|22_shizuoka|7274|Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property: Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori}} {{Shinto Navbox}} {{Shinto-stub}} {{citation needed|Kinomiya Jinja}} {{Draft categories| }} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{Source Wikipedia}} {{draft categories| }} {{draft categories| [[Category:Shinto shrines in Shizuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:History of Atami]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Atami]] [[Category:Yamato Takeru]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:beppyo shrines without templates]] [[Category:Son-sha]] [[Category:Kinomo]] [[Category:Atami, Shizuoka]] [[Category:cCompletion tier 2]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[Category:r]] [[Category:11]] [[Category:Pages from everybodywiki under right title]] [[Category:New]] }} [[sn:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[en:draft:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[en:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[ja:%E6%9D%A5%E5%AE%AE%E7%A5%9E%E7%A4%BE]] {{translated page|ja|来宮神社|version=104107598|comment=Imported full ja history}}

Wadō 3 (710) | honden = Nagare-zukuri style | festival = July 15 | ceremonies = Kogashi Matsuri (July 15–16) }} The [[Kinomiya Shrine]] is located in [[Atami]], [[Shizuoka (city)|Shizuoka]], and is famous for its natural treasures, especially the historic trees within its grounds.{{Cite web |last=Author |first=No |date=1999-12-08 |title=The natural treasures of Kinomiya Shrine |url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/1999/12/08/environment/the-natural-treasures-of-kinomiya-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-19 |website=The Japan Times |language=en}} It is located near [[Kinomiya Station]],{{Cite web |title=Expand your life expectancy at Kinomiya shrine, in Atami city｜TOMO – 供TOMO 玄米コーヒーオンラインストア |url=https://tomo.life/en/blogs/shinto-and-shrines/lets-visit-kinomiya-shrine |access-date=2023-10-19 |website=tomo.life}} and serves [[Amazake]]. [[File:Cinnamomum camphora 20100612 (Kinomiya Shrine) (B).jpg|thumb|The large camphor tree of Azusawake Jinja]] [[File:Cinnamomum camphora 20100612 (Kinomiya Shrine) (2nd).jpg|thumb|The second large camphor tree]] '''Kinomiya Jinja''' is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社|12=draft}} located in {{ill|Atami|ja|熱海市|lt=Atami City|12=draft}}, {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|ja|静岡県|lt=Shizuoka Prefecture|12=draft}}, Japan. Under the modern shrine Rank system, it was once a village shrine. == Shrine name == Historically known as “Kimiya Myōjin” or “Kinomiya Daimyōjin,” among others. After the Meiji Restoration, it was identified as the “Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja” (阿豆佐和気命神社) as a result of being associated with a Shikinaisha of that name. Later, when it was found that this was incorrect, it reverted to its current name.{{efn|However, pamphlets distributed by the shrine still state, “It is recorded in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō as ‘Azusawake Jinja.’”}} {{efn|Other candidates for Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja include a shrine of the same name in Toshima Village, Tokyo.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=http://www.tokyo-jinjacho.or.jp/tosho/2843/|title=Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja|publisher=Tokyo Jinja-chō|accessdate=2021-04-21}}}} == Enshrined Deities == * Yamato Takeru no Mikoto * Iitakeru no Mikoto (Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto = Isonotakeru?), identified as the wood (tree) deity Iitakeru (Itsu no Takeri). * Ōnamuchi no Mikoto (Ōkuninushi no Mikoto) In addition, Inari Jinja, Kakimoto-sha, and Tenjin-sha are enshrined in the same hall. The "Sōyuyama Engi (Sōyu-san Engi)" describes this shrine as the “jinushigami” (local guardian deity) of Izusan Jinja. Because “Kinomiya” can be interpreted as “I no Miya” meaning “忌の宮” (taboo shrine), many people come here to pray for abstinence from certain things (such as alcohol). == History == The founding time is unknown. According to shrine tradition, in Wadō 3 (710), fishermen found what seemed to be a divine wooden root caught in their fishing net three times in Atami Bay. They enshrined this root under a pine tree and offered roasted barley flour (mugi-kogashi). That night, Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto appeared in a dream, complaining about the noise of the sea, so they moved the deity to the current location in the forest. Because it was originally a wooden root, the shrine came to be called “Ki no Miya” (Kinomiya). This tradition strongly reflects “Kinomiya faith,” where driftwood or a piece of wood is worshiped, and Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto is revered as a wood (tree) deity. There is also a legend that Sakanoue no Tamuramaro prayed for victory here and enshrined divided spirits of this deity in various places in the Tohoku region. The shrine was a village shrine under the modern shrine system. After World War II, given its history and activities, it was added to the list of Beppyo Shrines under the Association of Shinto Shrines. [[File:Kinomiya jinja - March 7 2021 - various 14 58 24 831000.jpeg|thumb|Torii]] === Position in Atami City === Located in the hilly area near the center of the city, Kinomiya Jinja is considered a central shrine of the Atami area. Its festival, the Kogashi Matsuri (below), is Atami’s largest festival. It also performs rituals for many other shrines in Atami City that do not have their own resident priest. Only Izusan Jinja, Imamiya Jinja, and Ajiko Jinja have their own priests. Other shrines such as Misogino Taki Jinja, Meisui Jinja, Danna Jinja, Fujimori Inari Jinja, Yunomae Jinja, Goten Inari Jinja, Dairokuten-son Jinja, Tagajinja, Shimotaga Jinja, Tsushima Jinja, Koyama Shinmeigū, Wadanoki Jinja, and others are served by Kinomiya Jinja’s priests. Wada Hachiman Jinja’s rites are conducted by Imamiya Jinja’s priest, and Hatsuki Jinja on Hatsushima (an offshore island of Atami) is served by Izusan Jinja’s priest. As Atami’s tourism fortunes waned after the Bubble Economy collapse, pilgrimages to Kinomiya Jinja also declined. However, as Atami tourism recovered in the 2010s, Kinomiya Jinja also saw an increase in visitors. They introduced selfie stands, an open cafe, walking guides, and collaborated with local shops to create new sweets. In 2017, about 688,000 people visited, over four times the roughly 157,000 in 2008.[https://mainichi.jp/articles/20181203/dde/001/040/033000c “Check: Rebound with a Sacred Camphor Tree—Kinomiya Jinja in Atami leverages youth and female appeal”], Mainichi Shimbun (Evening edition), December 3, 2018, p.1. Accessed December 7, 2018. == Main festivals == === Kogashi Matsuri === * festival “Kogashi Matsuri” held around July 15 (including the eve on July 14 and events through July 16). Originally, as old lunar calendar June 15 was the day the fishermen discovered the wooden deity, they held the festival then, but in Meiji times it changed to the solar calendar.[http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/reitaisai.html festival] Kinomiya Jinja official site ** July 14: Eve festival (Yoi-miya-sai), praying for successful ceremonies. ** July 15: festival “Kogashi Matsuri” *** “Miya Mikoshi Togyo” (9:00–15:00): The shrine’s mikoshi visits Atami Station, Shinsui Park, Ginza-chō, and other city areas. *** “Reitaisai Hōhei” (11:00–): Offerings of mugikogashi (roasted barley flour), lily bulbs, bitter oranges, and tokoro jelly according to tradition. *** “Hōshuku Shinnei Gishiki” (11:40–13:00): Kashima Odori (Kashima dance), Miko Kagura (shrine maiden dance), Urayasu no Mai. *** “Kogashi Matsuri Dashi Contest” (18:30–21:30): About 30+ festival floats line up on National Route 135, which is closed off near Hotel Ōnoya through Atami Sun Beach, competing in a parade-style contest. ** July 16: *** “Jinkō-sai” (Shinkō-sai) **** “Hōshuku Shinnei Gishiki” (8:30–): Kashima Odori, Miko Kagura, Urayasu no Mai **** “Goshinkō Gyōretsu” (9:50–15:40): A procession of about 500 people including Tengu-masked, high-geta wearing Sarutahiko distributing mugikogashi (symbolizing rice), a Mikoshi, Shishimai (lion dance), priests, etc. They visit Yunomae Jinja, Atami Station, Sun Beach (with a mikoshi purification), Nagisa Kōen (with dances), and Ginza. At Ginza (in front of Ozawa Himono-ten[http://atamii.jp/today/73259/ Goshinkō parade in Atami city by Kinomiya Jinja concluding festival], Atami Net News, 2017/7/17), Kashima Odori is also performed. **** “Kanchōsai” (15:40–) *** “Kogashi Matsuri Dashi Contest” (18:30–21:00) === Setsubun festival === On Setsubun (February 3), a lively bean-throwing ceremony takes place with participating celebrities. Past participants include: * Izumi Pinko * Ehara Hiroyuki * Kuroda Arthur * Satō Yōko (violinist) * Nishikido Oyakata (former sumo wrestler Mitoizumi Masato) * Hashida Sugako * Hayashi Mariko * Motoki Daisuke == Shrine Buildings == The honden is nagare-zukuri style, connected with heiden and haiden in a gongen-zukuri arrangement. == Subsidiary Shrines == Within the precincts: * Kinomiya Inari-sha (Inari shrine from Fushimi Inari Taisha in Kyoto) * Kinomiya Benzaiten (Benzaiten statue by Takamura Kōun is shown on November 23) * Mitsumine Jinja [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/top/setsumassha.html Kinomiya Jinja – Subsidiary Shrines] (Accessed December 7, 2018) == Cultural Properties == [[File:Azusawake Jinja no Okusu -02.jpg|thumb|150px|Great Camphor Tree of Azusawake Jinja]] === National Natural Monument === {{Main|{{ill|Azusawake Jinja no Ōkusu|ja|阿豆佐和気神社の大クス|12=draft}}|{{ill|Kamanariya Heishichi|ja|釜鳴屋平七|12=draft}}}} * The Great Camphor Tree of Azusawake Jinja (over 2000 years old, trunk circumference about 24m, height 20m), designated in Shōwa 8. Circling it once is said to extend life by one year or grant wishes. Historically, seven camphor trees stood here, but during the Ansei era (1855–60), a dispute related to fishing rights (the Ōami/maguro-ami incident) forced them to cut five for lawsuit costs.[https://www.city.atami.lg.jp/kosodate/shogaigakushu/1011165/1006016/1009091/1009107.html Episode 14: Local Hero Kamanariya Heishichi] - Atami City Hall[http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/supporting_party/ 50th Anniversary of Iitakeru no Mikoto’s 1300th Enshrinement: Rebuilding Senshūden and Grounds Improvement Project] - Kinomiya Jinja Another large camphor stands near the entrance. === Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property === * Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori (Kashima dance) Performed during the Kogashi Matsuri at the shrine grounds, Atami Station front, Nagisa Kōen, and Ginza Street. The dancers carry ladles with colored papers symbolizing rice grains, praying for abundant harvest and warding off evil. It’s recognized as a Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property. {{citation needed|Kinomiya Jinja}} == Trees == Horuto-no-ki ([[Elaeocarpus sylvestris|Elaeacarpus sylvestris var. ellipticus]]): A unique evergreen species rare to Japan. Characterized by smooth gray bark and leathery leaves, it produces white flowers in July or August. Its leaves turn red before shedding. Two species of this genus grow wild in the warm temperate regions of Japan. Kinomiya no O-kusu (Camphor Tree, Cinnamomum camphora): This colossal tree, standing 23 meters in circumference and estimated to be over 2,000 years old, is recognized as Japan's second largest and oldest kusunoki tree. Known as Goshinboku, or the Holy Tree, it's believed that a Shinto god resides within it. Many believe the tree possesses special powers, granting health, safety, and longevity to those who visit. The bark of this tree is brown and lightly fissured, and its wood is often used in furniture and sculpture. Extracts from the leaves of this tree have medicinal uses in Chinese medicine. It is designated as a natural monument. == Other natural treasures == Beyond the Kinomiya Shrine, other notable trees include Japan's largest camphor tree located at a Hachiman Shrine in Kamo-cho, Kagoshima, and the oldest tree in Japan, a 3,000-year-old kusunoki found in Saga Prefecture. The Kinomiya Shrine is surrounded by a woodland which can be classified as a small laurel forest or ''shoyo-juinrin''. Many trees in this forest are broadleaf evergreens, safeguarding aspects of the local flora from development. == Other == * In May 2011, a 300-year-old holly oak tree next to the torii toppled at its base and damaged the 1920s torii. == Access == * About a 5-minute walk from [[Kinomiya Station]] (JR Itō Line). Also walkable (about 18 minutes) from [[Atami Station]] or reachable by city bus (Ten Nation Pass line or Nishiyama loop) to “Kinomiya Jinja Mae” bus stop.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/praying/access/|title=Access|publisher=Kinomiya Jinja|accessdate=2021-04-21}} The shrine grounds are open from 9:00 to 17:00. == References == * Tanigawa Ken’ichi ed., "Nihon no Kami, Jinja to Seichi Vol.10 Tōkai", Hakusuisha, 1987 == See Also == * Kinomiya faith * Kashima Odori == Notes == === Notes === {{notelist}} === Sources === {{Reflist|2}} == External Links == {{commonscat|Kinomiya-jinja}} * [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/ Official Website of Kinomiya Jinja] * [https://atami.travel/atami-tourism/kinomiya-shrin/ Atami Tourism Bureau - Kinomiya Jinja] * {{Cultural Heritage Online|22_shizuoka|7274|Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property: Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori}} {{Shinto Navbox}} {{Shinto-stub}} {{citation needed|Kinomiya Jinja}} {{Draft categories| }} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{Source Wikipedia}} {{draft categories| }} {{draft categories| }} {{translated page|ja|来宮神社|version=104107598|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 7]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Shizuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:History of Atami]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Atami]] [[Category:Yamato Takeru]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:beppyo shrines without templates]] [[Category:Son-sha]] [[Category:Kinomo]] [[Category:Atami, Shizuoka]] [[Category:cCompletion tier 2]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[Category:r]] [[Category:Pages from everybodywiki under right title]] }} [[sn:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[en:draft:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[en:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[ja:%E6%9D%A5%E5%AE%AE%E7%A5%9E%E7%A4%BE]]

It is designated as a natural monument. == Other natural treasures == Beyond the Kinomiya Shrine, other notable trees include Japan's largest camphor tree located at a Hachiman Shrine in Kamo-cho, Kagoshima, and the oldest tree in Japan, a 3,000-year-old kusunoki found in Saga Prefecture. The Kinomiya Shrine is surrounded by a woodland which can be classified as a small laurel forest or ''shoyo-juinrin''. Many trees in this forest are broadleaf evergreens, safeguarding aspects of the local flora from development. == Other == * In May 2011, a 300-year-old holly oak tree next to the torii toppled at its base and damaged the 1920s torii. == Access == * About a 5-minute walk from [[Kinomiya Station]] (JR Itō Line). Also walkable (about 18 minutes) from [[Atami Station]] or reachable by city bus (Ten Nation Pass line or Nishiyama loop) to “Kinomiya Jinja Mae” bus stop.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/praying/access/|title=Access|publisher=Kinomiya Jinja|accessdate=2021-04-21}} The shrine grounds are open from 9:00 to 17:00. == References == * Tanigawa Ken’ichi ed., "Nihon no Kami, Jinja to Seichi Vol.10 Tōkai", Hakusuisha, 1987 == See Also == * Kinomiya faith * Kashima Odori == Notes == === Notes === {{notelist}} === Sources === {{Reflist|2}} == External Links == {{commonscat|Kinomiya-jinja}} * [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/ Official Website of Kinomiya Jinja] * [https://atami.travel/atami-tourism/kinomiya-shrin/ Atami Tourism Bureau - Kinomiya Jinja] * {{Cultural Heritage Online|22_shizuoka|7274|Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property: Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori}} {{Shinto Navbox}} {{Shinto-stub}} {{citation needed|Kinomiya Jinja}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{Source Wikipedia}} {{translated page|ja|来宮神社|version=104107598|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 7]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Shizuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:History of Atami]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Atami]] [[Category:Yamato Takeru]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:beppyo shrines without templates]] [[Category:Son-sha]] [[Category:Kinomo]] [[Category:Atami, Shizuoka]] [[Category:cCompletion tier 2]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[Category:r]] [[Category:Pages from everybodywiki under right title]] }} [[every:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[sn:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[en:draft:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[en:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[ja:%E6%9D%A5%E5%AE%AE%E7%A5%9E%E7%A4%BE]]

Wadō 3 (710) | honden = Nagare-zukuri style | festival = July 15 | ceremonies = Kogashi Matsuri (July 15–16) }} The [[Kinomiya Shrine]] is located in [[Atami]], [[Shizuoka (city)|Shizuoka]], and is famous for its natural treasures, especially the historic trees within its grounds.{{Cite web |last=Author |first=No |date=1999-12-08 |title=The natural treasures of Kinomiya Shrine |url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/1999/12/08/environment/the-natural-treasures-of-kinomiya-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-19 |website=The Japan Times |language=en}} It is located near [[Kinomiya Station]],{{Cite web |title=Expand your life expectancy at Kinomiya shrine, in Atami city｜TOMO – 供TOMO 玄米コーヒーオンラインストア |url=https://tomo.life/en/blogs/shinto-and-shrines/lets-visit-kinomiya-shrine |access-date=2023-10-19 |website=tomo.life}} and serves [[Amazake]]. [[File:Cinnamomum camphora 20100612 (Kinomiya Shrine) (B).jpg|thumb|The large camphor tree of Azusawake Jinja]] [[File:Cinnamomum camphora 20100612 (Kinomiya Shrine) (2nd).jpg|thumb|The second large camphor tree]] '''Kinomiya Jinja''' is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社|qq=draft}} located in {{ill|Atami|ja|熱海市|lt=Atami City|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|ja|静岡県|lt=Shizuoka Prefecture|qq=draft}}, Japan. Under the modern shrine Rank system, it was once a village shrine. == Shrine name == Historically known as “Kimiya Myōjin” or “Kinomiya Daimyōjin,” among others. After the Meiji Restoration, it was identified as the “Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja” (阿豆佐和気命神社) as a result of being associated with a Shikinaisha of that name. Later, when it was found that this was incorrect, it reverted to its current name.{{efn|However, pamphlets distributed by the shrine still state, “It is recorded in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō as ‘Azusawake Jinja.’”}} {{efn|Other candidates for Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja include a shrine of the same name in Toshima Village, Tokyo.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=http://www.tokyo-jinjacho.or.jp/tosho/2843/|title=Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja|publisher=Tokyo Jinja-chō|accessdate=2021-04-21}}}} == Enshrined Deities == * Yamato Takeru no Mikoto * Iitakeru no Mikoto (Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto = Isonotakeru?), identified as the wood (tree) deity Iitakeru (Itsu no Takeri). * Ōnamuchi no Mikoto (Ōkuninushi no Mikoto) In addition, Inari Jinja, Kakimoto-sha, and Tenjin-sha are enshrined in the same hall. The "Sōyuyama Engi (Sōyu-san Engi)" describes this shrine as the “jinushigami” (local guardian deity) of Izusan Jinja. Because “Kinomiya” can be interpreted as “I no Miya” meaning “忌の宮” (taboo shrine), many people come here to pray for abstinence from certain things (such as alcohol). == History == The founding time is unknown. According to shrine tradition, in Wadō 3 (710), fishermen found what seemed to be a divine wooden root caught in their fishing net three times in Atami Bay. They enshrined this root under a pine tree and offered roasted barley flour (mugi-kogashi). That night, Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto appeared in a dream, complaining about the noise of the sea, so they moved the deity to the current location in the forest. Because it was originally a wooden root, the shrine came to be called “Ki no Miya” (Kinomiya). This tradition strongly reflects “Kinomiya faith,” where driftwood or a piece of wood is worshiped, and Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto is revered as a wood (tree) deity. There is also a legend that Sakanoue no Tamuramaro prayed for victory here and enshrined divided spirits of this deity in various places in the Tohoku region. The shrine was a village shrine under the modern shrine system. After World War II, given its history and activities, it was added to the list of Beppyo Shrines under the Association of Shinto Shrines. [[File:Kinomiya jinja - March 7 2021 - various 14 58 24 831000.jpeg|thumb|Torii]] === Position in Atami City === Located in the hilly area near the center of the city, Kinomiya Jinja is considered a central shrine of the Atami area. Its festival, the Kogashi Matsuri (below), is Atami’s largest festival. It also performs rituals for many other shrines in Atami City that do not have their own resident priest. Only Izusan Jinja, Imamiya Jinja, and Ajiko Jinja have their own priests. Other shrines such as Misogino Taki Jinja, Meisui Jinja, Danna Jinja, Fujimori Inari Jinja, Yunomae Jinja, Goten Inari Jinja, Dairokuten-son Jinja, Tagajinja, Shimotaga Jinja, Tsushima Jinja, Koyama Shinmeigū, Wadanoki Jinja, and others are served by Kinomiya Jinja’s priests. Wada Hachiman Jinja’s rites are conducted by Imamiya Jinja’s priest, and Hatsuki Jinja on Hatsushima (an offshore island of Atami) is served by Izusan Jinja’s priest. As Atami’s tourism fortunes waned after the Bubble Economy collapse, pilgrimages to Kinomiya Jinja also declined. However, as Atami tourism recovered in the 2010s, Kinomiya Jinja also saw an increase in visitors. They introduced selfie stands, an open cafe, walking guides, and collaborated with local shops to create new sweets. In 2017, about 688,000 people visited, over four times the roughly 157,000 in 2008.[https://mainichi.jp/articles/20181203/dde/001/040/033000c “Check: Rebound with a Sacred Camphor Tree—Kinomiya Jinja in Atami leverages youth and female appeal”], Mainichi Shimbun (Evening edition), December 3, 2018, p.1. Accessed December 7, 2018. == Main festivals == === Kogashi Matsuri === * festival “Kogashi Matsuri” held around July 15 (including the eve on July 14 and events through July 16). Originally, as old lunar calendar June 15 was the day the fishermen discovered the wooden deity, they held the festival then, but in Meiji times it changed to the solar calendar.[http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/reitaisai.html festival] Kinomiya Jinja official site ** July 14: Eve festival (Yoi-miya-sai), praying for successful ceremonies. ** July 15: festival “Kogashi Matsuri” *** “Miya Mikoshi Togyo” (9:00–15:00): The shrine’s mikoshi visits Atami Station, Shinsui Park, Ginza-chō, and other city areas. *** “Reitaisai Hōhei” (11:00–): Offerings of mugikogashi (roasted barley flour), lily bulbs, bitter oranges, and tokoro jelly according to tradition. *** “Hōshuku Shinnei Gishiki” (11:40–13:00): Kashima Odori (Kashima dance), Miko Kagura (shrine maiden dance), Urayasu no Mai. *** “Kogashi Matsuri Dashi Contest” (18:30–21:30): About 30+ festival floats line up on National Route 135, which is closed off near Hotel Ōnoya through Atami Sun Beach, competing in a parade-style contest. ** July 16: *** “Jinkō-sai” (Shinkō-sai) **** “Hōshuku Shinnei Gishiki” (8:30–): Kashima Odori, Miko Kagura, Urayasu no Mai **** “Goshinkō Gyōretsu” (9:50–15:40): A procession of about 500 people including Tengu-masked, high-geta wearing Sarutahiko distributing mugikogashi (symbolizing rice), a Mikoshi, Shishimai (lion dance), priests, etc. They visit Yunomae Jinja, Atami Station, Sun Beach (with a mikoshi purification), Nagisa Kōen (with dances), and Ginza. At Ginza (in front of Ozawa Himono-ten[http://atamii.jp/today/73259/ Goshinkō parade in Atami city by Kinomiya Jinja concluding festival], Atami Net News, 2017/7/17), Kashima Odori is also performed. **** “Kanchōsai” (15:40–) *** “Kogashi Matsuri Dashi Contest” (18:30–21:00) === Setsubun festival === On Setsubun (February 3), a lively bean-throwing ceremony takes place with participating celebrities. Past participants include: * Izumi Pinko * Ehara Hiroyuki * Kuroda Arthur * Satō Yōko (violinist) * Nishikido Oyakata (former sumo wrestler Mitoizumi Masato) * Hashida Sugako * Hayashi Mariko * Motoki Daisuke == Shrine Buildings == The honden is nagare-zukuri style, connected with heiden and haiden in a gongen-zukuri arrangement. == Subsidiary Shrines == Within the precincts: * Kinomiya Inari-sha (Inari shrine from Fushimi Inari Taisha in Kyoto) * Kinomiya Benzaiten (Benzaiten statue by Takamura Kōun is shown on November 23) * Mitsumine Jinja [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/top/setsumassha.html Kinomiya Jinja – Subsidiary Shrines] (Accessed December 7, 2018) == Cultural Properties == [[File:Azusawake Jinja no Okusu -02.jpg|thumb|150px|Great Camphor Tree of Azusawake Jinja]] === National Natural Monument === {{Main|{{ill|Azusawake Jinja no Ōkusu|ja|阿豆佐和気神社の大クス|qq=draft}}|{{ill|Kamanariya Heishichi|ja|釜鳴屋平七|qq=draft}}}} * The Great Camphor Tree of Azusawake Jinja (over 2000 years old, trunk circumference about 24m, height 20m), designated in Shōwa 8. Circling it once is said to extend life by one year or grant wishes. Historically, seven camphor trees stood here, but during the Ansei era (1855–60), a dispute related to fishing rights (the Ōami/maguro-ami incident) forced them to cut five for lawsuit costs.[https://www.city.atami.lg.jp/kosodate/shogaigakushu/1011165/1006016/1009091/1009107.html Episode 14: Local Hero Kamanariya Heishichi] - Atami City Hall[http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/supporting_party/ 50th Anniversary of Iitakeru no Mikoto’s 1300th Enshrinement: Rebuilding Senshūden and Grounds Improvement Project] - Kinomiya Jinja Another large camphor stands near the entrance. === Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property === * Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori (Kashima dance) Performed during the Kogashi Matsuri at the shrine grounds, Atami Station front, Nagisa Kōen, and Ginza Street. The dancers carry ladles with colored papers symbolizing rice grains, praying for abundant harvest and warding off evil. It’s recognized as a Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property. {{citation needed|Kinomiya Jinja}} == Trees == Horuto-no-ki ([[Elaeocarpus sylvestris|Elaeacarpus sylvestris var. ellipticus]]): A unique evergreen species rare to Japan. Characterized by smooth gray bark and leathery leaves, it produces white flowers in July or August. Its leaves turn red before shedding. Two species of this genus grow wild in the warm temperate regions of Japan. Kinomiya no O-kusu (Camphor Tree, Cinnamomum camphora): This colossal tree, standing 23 meters in circumference and estimated to be over 2,000 years old, is recognized as Japan's second largest and oldest kusunoki tree. Known as Goshinboku, or the Holy Tree, it's believed that a Shinto god resides within it. Many believe the tree possesses special powers, granting health, safety, and longevity to those who visit. The bark of this tree is brown and lightly fissured, and its wood is often used in furniture and sculpture. Extracts from the leaves of this tree have medicinal uses in Chinese medicine. It is designated as a natural monument. == Other natural treasures == Beyond the Kinomiya Shrine, other notable trees include Japan's largest camphor tree located at a Hachiman Shrine in Kamo-cho, Kagoshima, and the oldest tree in Japan, a 3,000-year-old kusunoki found in Saga Prefecture. The Kinomiya Shrine is surrounded by a woodland which can be classified as a small laurel forest or ''shoyo-juinrin''. Many trees in this forest are broadleaf evergreens, safeguarding aspects of the local flora from development. == Other == * In May 2011, a 300-year-old holly oak tree next to the torii toppled at its base and damaged the 1920s torii. == Access == * About a 5-minute walk from [[Kinomiya Station]] (JR Itō Line). Also walkable (about 18 minutes) from [[Atami Station]] or reachable by city bus (Ten Nation Pass line or Nishiyama loop) to “Kinomiya Jinja Mae” bus stop.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/praying/access/|title=Access|publisher=Kinomiya Jinja|accessdate=2021-04-21}} The shrine grounds are open from 9:00 to 17:00. == References == * Tanigawa Ken’ichi ed., "Nihon no Kami, Jinja to Seichi Vol.10 Tōkai", Hakusuisha, 1987 == See Also == * Kinomiya faith * Kashima Odori == Notes == === Notes === {{notelist}} === Sources === {{Reflist|2}} == External Links == {{commonscat|Kinomiya-jinja}} * [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/ Official Website of Kinomiya Jinja] * [https://atami.travel/atami-tourism/kinomiya-shrin/ Atami Tourism Bureau - Kinomiya Jinja] * {{Cultural Heritage Online|22_shizuoka|7274|Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property: Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori}} {{Shinto Navbox}} {{Shinto-stub}} {{citation needed|Kinomiya Jinja}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{Source Wikipedia}} {{translated page|ja|来宮神社|version=104107598|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 7]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Shizuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:History of Atami]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Atami]] [[Category:Yamato Takeru]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:beppyo shrines without templates]] [[Category:Son-sha]] [[Category:Kinomo]] [[Category:Atami, Shizuoka]] [[Category:cCompletion tier 2]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[Category:r]] [[Category:Pages from everybodywiki under right title]] }} [[every:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[sn:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[en:draft:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[en:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[ja:%E6%9D%A5%E5%AE%AE%E7%A5%9E%E7%A4%BE]]

Originally, as old lunar calendar June 15 was the day the fishermen discovered the wooden deity, they held the festival then, but in Meiji times it changed to the solar calendar.[http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/reitaisai.html festival] Kinomiya Jinja official site ** July 14: Eve festival (Yoi-miya-sai), praying for successful ceremonies. ** July 15: festival “Kogashi Matsuri” *** “Miya Mikoshi Togyo” (9:00–15:00): The shrine’s mikoshi visits Atami Station, Shinsui Park, Ginza-chō, and other city areas. *** “Reitaisai Hōhei” (11:00–): Offerings of mugikogashi (roasted barley flour), lily bulbs, bitter oranges, and tokoro jelly according to tradition. *** “Hōshuku Shinnei Gishiki” (11:40–13:00): Kashima Odori (Kashima dance), Miko Kagura (shrine maiden dance), Urayasu no Mai. *** “Kogashi Matsuri Dashi Contest” (18:30–21:30): About 30+ festival floats line up on National Route 135, which is closed off near Hotel Ōnoya through Atami Sun Beach, competing in a parade-style contest. ** July 16: *** “Jinkō-sai” (Shinkō-sai) **** “Hōshuku Shinnei Gishiki” (8:30–): Kashima Odori, Miko Kagura, Urayasu no Mai **** “Goshinkō Gyōretsu” (9:50–15:40): A procession of about 500 people including Tengu-masked, high-geta wearing Sarutahiko distributing mugikogashi (symbolizing rice), a Mikoshi, Shishimai (lion dance), priests, etc. They visit Yunomae Jinja, Atami Station, Sun Beach (with a mikoshi purification), Nagisa Kōen (with dances), and Ginza. At Ginza (in front of Ozawa Himono-ten[http://atamii.jp/today/73259/ Goshinkō parade in Atami city by Kinomiya Jinja concluding festival], Atami Net News, 2017/7/17), Kashima Odori is also performed. **** “Kanchōsai” (15:40–) *** “Kogashi Matsuri Dashi Contest” (18:30–21:00) === Setsubun festival === On Setsubun (February 3), a lively bean-throwing ceremony takes place with participating celebrities. Past participants include: * Izumi Pinko * Ehara Hiroyuki * Kuroda Arthur * Satō Yōko (violinist) * Nishikido Oyakata (former sumo wrestler Mitoizumi Masato) * Hashida Sugako * Hayashi Mariko * Motoki Daisuke == Shrine Buildings == The honden is nagare-zukuri style, connected with heiden and haiden in a gongen-zukuri arrangement. == Subsidiary Shrines == Within the precincts: * Kinomiya Inari-sha (Inari shrine from Fushimi Inari Taisha in Kyoto) * Kinomiya Benzaiten (Benzaiten statue by Takamura Kōun is shown on November 23) * Mitsumine Jinja [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/top/setsumassha.html Kinomiya Jinja – Subsidiary Shrines] (Accessed December 7, 2018) == Cultural Properties == [[File:Azusawake Jinja no Okusu -02.jpg|thumb|150px|Great Camphor Tree of Azusawake Jinja]] === National Natural Monument === {{Main|{{ill|Azusawake Jinja no Ōkusu|ja|阿豆佐和気神社の大クス|qq=draft}}|{{ill|Kamanariya Heishichi|ja|釜鳴屋平七|qq=draft}}}} * The Great Camphor Tree of Azusawake Jinja (over 2000 years old, trunk circumference about 24m, height 20m), designated in Shōwa 8. Circling it once is said to extend life by one year or grant wishes. Historically, seven camphor trees stood here, but during the Ansei era (1855–60), a dispute related to fishing rights (the Ōami/maguro-ami incident) forced them to cut five for lawsuit costs.[https://www.city.atami.lg.jp/kosodate/shogaigakushu/1011165/1006016/1009091/1009107.html Episode 14: Local Hero Kamanariya Heishichi] - Atami City Hall[http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/supporting_party/ 50th Anniversary of Iitakeru no Mikoto’s 1300th Enshrinement: Rebuilding Senshūden and Grounds Improvement Project] - Kinomiya Jinja Another large camphor stands near the entrance. === Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property === * Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori (Kashima dance) Performed during the Kogashi Matsuri at the shrine grounds, Atami Station front, Nagisa Kōen, and Ginza Street. The dancers carry ladles with colored papers symbolizing rice grains, praying for abundant harvest and warding off evil. It’s recognized as a Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property. {{citation needed|Kinomiya Jinja}} == Trees == Horuto-no-ki ([[Elaeocarpus sylvestris|Elaeacarpus sylvestris var. ellipticus]]): A unique evergreen species rare to Japan. Characterized by smooth gray bark and leathery leaves, it produces white flowers in July or August. Its leaves turn red before shedding. Two species of this genus grow wild in the warm temperate regions of Japan. Kinomiya no O-kusu (Camphor Tree, Cinnamomum camphora): This colossal tree, standing 23 meters in circumference and estimated to be over 2,000 years old, is recognized as Japan's second largest and oldest kusunoki tree. Known as Goshinboku, or the Holy Tree, it's believed that a Shinto god resides within it. Many believe the tree possesses special powers, granting health, safety, and longevity to those who visit. The bark of this tree is brown and lightly fissured, and its wood is often used in furniture and sculpture. Extracts from the leaves of this tree have medicinal uses in Chinese medicine. It is designated as a natural monument. == Other natural treasures == Beyond the Kinomiya Shrine, other notable trees include Japan's largest camphor tree located at a Hachiman Shrine in Kamo-cho, Kagoshima, and the oldest tree in Japan, a 3,000-year-old kusunoki found in Saga Prefecture. The Kinomiya Shrine is surrounded by a woodland which can be classified as a small laurel forest or ''shoyo-juinrin''. Many trees in this forest are broadleaf evergreens, safeguarding aspects of the local flora from development. == Other == * In May 2011, a 300-year-old holly oak tree next to the torii toppled at its base and damaged the 1920s torii. == Access == * About a 5-minute walk from [[Kinomiya Station]] (JR Itō Line). Also walkable (about 18 minutes) from [[Atami Station]] or reachable by city bus (Ten Nation Pass line or Nishiyama loop) to “Kinomiya Jinja Mae” bus stop.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/praying/access/|title=Access|publisher=Kinomiya Jinja|accessdate=2021-04-21}} The shrine grounds are open from 9:00 to 17:00. == References == * Tanigawa Ken’ichi ed., "Nihon no Kami, Jinja to Seichi Vol.10 Tōkai", Hakusuisha, 1987 == See Also == * Kinomiya faith * Kashima Odori == Notes == === Notes === {{notelist}} === Sources === {{Reflist|2}} == External Links == {{commonscat|Kinomiya-jinja}} * [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/ Official Website of Kinomiya Jinja] * [https://atami.travel/atami-tourism/kinomiya-shrin/ Atami Tourism Bureau - Kinomiya Jinja] * {{Cultural Heritage Online|22_shizuoka|7274|Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property: Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori}} {{Shinto Navbox}} {{Shinto-stub}} {{citation needed|Kinomiya Jinja}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{Source Wikipedia}} {{translated page|ja|来宮神社|version=104107598|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 7]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Shizuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:History of Atami]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Atami]] [[Category:Yamato Takeru]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:beppyo shrines without templates]] [[Category:Son-sha]] [[Category:Kinomo]] [[Category:Atami, Shizuoka]] [[Category:cCompletion tier 2]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[Category:r]] [[Category:Pages from everybodywiki under right title]] }} [[every:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[sn:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[en:draft:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[en:Kinomiya Shrine]] [[ja:%E6%9D%A5%E5%AE%AE%E7%A5%9E%E7%A4%BE]]
