Wadō 3 (710) | honden = Nagare-zukuri style | festival = July 15 | ceremonies = Kogashi Matsuri (July 15–16) }} The [[Kinomiya Shrine]] is located in [[:en:Atami|Atami]], [[:en:Shizuoka (city)|Shizuoka]], and is famous for its natural treasures, especially the historic trees within its grounds.{{Cite web |last=Author |first=No |date=1999-12-08 |title=The natural treasures of Kinomiya Shrine |url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/1999/12/08/environment/the-natural-treasures-of-kinomiya-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-19 |website=The Japan Times |language=en}} It is located near [[:en:Kinomiya Station|Kinomiya Station]],{{Cite web |title=Expand your life expectancy at Kinomiya shrine, in Atami city｜TOMO – 供TOMO 玄米コーヒーオンラインストア |url=https://tomo.life/en/blogs/shinto-and-shrines/lets-visit-kinomiya-shrine |access-date=2023-10-19 |website=tomo.life}} and serves [[Amazake]]. [[File:Cinnamomum camphora 20100612 (Kinomiya Shrine) (B).jpg|thumb|The large camphor tree of Azusawake Jinja]] [[File:Cinnamomum camphora 20100612 (Kinomiya Shrine) (2nd).jpg|thumb|The second large camphor tree]] '''Kinomiya Jinja''' is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in [[:en:Atami|Atami City]], [[:en:Shizuoka Prefecture|Shizuoka Prefecture]], Japan. Under the modern shrine Rank system, it was once a village shrine. == Shrine name == Historically known as “Kimiya Myōjin” or “Kinomiya Daimyōjin,” among others. After the Meiji Restoration, it was identified as the “Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja” (阿豆佐和気命神社) as a result of being associated with a Shikinaisha in that name. Later, when it was found that this was incorrect, it reverted to its current name.{{efn|However, pamphlets distributed by the shrine still state, “It is recorded in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō as ‘Azusawake Jinja.’”}} {{efn|Other candidates for Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja include a shrine of the same name in Toshima Village, Tokyo.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=http://www.tokyo-jinjacho.or.jp/tosho/2843/|title=Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja|publisher=Tokyo Jinja-chō|accessdate=2021-04-21}}}} == Enshrined Deities == * Yamato Takeru no Mikoto * Iitakeru no Mikoto (Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto = Isonotakeru?), identified as the wood (tree) deity Iitakeru (Itsu no Takeri). * Ōnamuchi no Mikoto (Ōkuninushi no Mikoto) In addition, Inari Jinja, Kakimoto-sha, and Tenjin-sha are enshrined in the same hall. The "Sōyuyama Engi (Sōyu-san Engi)" describes this shrine as the “jinushigami” (local guardian deity) of Izusan Jinja. Because “Kinomiya” can be interpreted as “I no Miya” meaning “忌の宮” (taboo shrine), many people come here to pray for abstinence from certain things (such as alcohol). == History == The founding time is unknown. According to shrine tradition, in Wadō 3 (710), fishermen found what seemed to be a divine wooden root caught in their fishing net three times in Atami Bay. They enshrined this root under a pine tree and offered roasted barley flour (mugi-kogashi). That night, Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto appeared in a dream, complaining about the noise of the sea, so they moved the deity to the current location in the forest. Because it was originally a wooden root, the shrine came to be called “Ki no Miya” (Kinomiya). This tradition strongly reflects “Kinomiya faith,” where driftwood or a piece of wood is worshiped, and Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto is revered as a wood (tree) deity. There is also a legend that Sakanoue no Tamuramaro prayed for victory here and enshrined divided spirits of this deity in various places in the Tohoku region. The shrine was a village shrine under the modern shrine system. After World War II, given its history and activities, it was added to the list of Beppyo Shrines under the Association of Shinto Shrines. [[File:Kinomiya jinja - March 7 2021 - various 14 58 24 831000.jpeg|thumb|Torii]] === Position in Atami City === Located in the hilly area near the center of the city, Kinomiya Jinja is considered a central shrine of the Atami area. Its festival, the Kogashi Matsuri (below), is Atami’s largest festival. It also performs rituals for many other shrines in Atami City that do not have their own resident priest. Only Izusan Jinja, Imamiya Jinja, and Ajiko Jinja have their own priests. Other shrines such as Misogino Taki Jinja, Meisui Jinja, Danna Jinja, Fujimori Inari Jinja, Yunomae Jinja, Goten Inari Jinja, Dairokuten-son Jinja, Tagajinja, Shimotaga Jinja, Tsushima Jinja, Koyama Shinmeigū, Wadanoki Jinja, and others are served by Kinomiya Jinja’s priests. Wada Hachiman Jinja’s rites are conducted by Imamiya Jinja’s priest, and Hatsuki Jinja on Hatsushima (an offshore island of Atami) is served by Izusan Jinja’s priest. As Atami’s tourism fortunes waned after the Bubble Economy collapse, pilgrimages to Kinomiya Jinja also declined. However, as Atami tourism recovered in the 2010s, Kinomiya Jinja also saw an increase in visitors. They introduced selfie stands, an open cafe, walking guides, and collaborated with local shops to create new sweets. In 2017, about 688,000 people visited, over four times the roughly 157,000 in 2008.[https://mainichi.jp/articles/20181203/dde/001/040/033000c “Check: Rebound with a Sacred Camphor Tree—Kinomiya Jinja in Atami leverages youth and female appeal”], Mainichi Shimbun (Evening edition), December 3, 2018, p.1. Accessed December 7, 2018. == Main festivals == === Kogashi Matsuri === * festival “Kogashi Matsuri” held around July 15 (including the eve on July 14 and events through July 16). Originally, as old lunar calendar June 15 was the day the fishermen discovered the wooden deity, they held the festival then, but in Meiji times it changed to the solar calendar.[http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/reitaisai.html festival] Kinomiya Jinja official site ** July 14: Eve festival (Yoi-miya-sai), praying for successful ceremonies. ** July 15: festival “Kogashi Matsuri” *** “Miya Mikoshi Togyo” (9:00–15:00): The shrine’s mikoshi visits Atami Station, Shinsui Park, Ginza-chō, and other city areas. *** “Reitaisai Hōhei” (11:00–): Offerings of mugikogashi (roasted barley flour), lily bulbs, bitter oranges, and tokoro jelly according to tradition. *** “Hōshuku Shinnei Gishiki” (11:40–13:00): Kashima Odori (Kashima dance), Miko Kagura (shrine maiden dance), Urayasu no Mai. *** “Kogashi Matsuri Dashi Contest” (18:30–21:30): About 30+ festival floats line up on National Route 135, which is closed off near Hotel Ōnoya through Atami Sun Beach, competing in a parade-style contest. ** July 16: *** “Jinkō-sai” (Shinkō-sai) **** “Hōshuku Shinnei Gishiki” (8:30–): Kashima Odori, Miko Kagura, Urayasu no Mai **** “Goshinkō Gyōretsu” (9:50–15:40): A procession of about 500 people including Tengu-masked, high-geta wearing Sarutahiko distributing mugikogashi (symbolizing rice), a Mikoshi, Shishimai (lion dance), priests, etc. They visit Yunomae Jinja, Atami Station, Sun Beach (with a mikoshi purification), Nagisa Kōen (with dances), and Ginza. At Ginza (in front of Ozawa Himono-ten[http://atamii.jp/today/73259/ Goshinkō parade in Atami city by Kinomiya Jinja concluding festival], Atami Net News, 2017/7/17), Kashima Odori is also performed. **** “Kanchōsai” (15:40–) *** “Kogashi Matsuri Dashi Contest” (18:30–21:00) === Setsubun festival === On Setsubun (February 3), a lively bean-throwing ceremony takes place with participating celebrities. Past participants include: * Izumi Pinko * Ehara Hiroyuki * Kuroda Arthur * Satō Yōko (violinist) * Nishikido Oyakata (former sumo wrestler Mitoizumi Masato) * Hashida Sugako * Hayashi Mariko * Motoki Daisuke == Shrine Buildings == The honden is nagare-zukuri style, connected with heiden and haiden in a gongen-zukuri arrangement. == Subsidiary Shrines == Within the precincts: * Kinomiya Inari-sha (Inari shrine from Fushimi Inari Taisha in Kyoto) * Kinomiya Benzaiten (Benzaiten statue by Takamura Kōun is shown on November 23) * Mitsumine Jinja [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/top/setsumassha.html Kinomiya Jinja – Subsidiary Shrines] (Accessed December 7, 2018) == Cultural Properties == [[File:Azusawake Jinja no Okusu -02.jpg|thumb|150px|Great Camphor Tree of Azusawake Jinja]] === National Natural Monument === {{Main|{{ill|Azusawake Jinja no Ōkusu|ja|阿豆佐和気神社の大クス|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Azusawake Jinja no Ōkusu|qq=|1=Azusawakejinja-no-Okusu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q60403026}}|{{ill|Kamanariya Heishichi|ja|釜鳴屋平七|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamanariya Heishichi|qq=|1=kamanariya heishichi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q65289080}}}} * The Great Camphor Tree of Azusawake Jinja (over 2000 years old, trunk circumference about 24m, height 20m), designated in Shōwa 8. Circling it once is said to extend life by one year or grant wishes. Historically, seven camphor trees stood here, but during the Ansei era (1855–60), a dispute related to fishing rights (the Ōami/maguro-ami incident) forced them to cut five for lawsuit costs.[https://www.city.atami.lg.jp/kosodate/shogaigakushu/1011165/1006016/1009091/1009107.html Episode 14: Local Hero Kamanariya Heishichi] - Atami City Hall[http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/supporting_party/ 50th Anniversary of Iitakeru no Mikoto’s 1300th Enshrinement: Rebuilding Senshūden and Grounds Improvement Project] - Kinomiya Jinja Another large camphor stands near the entrance. === Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property === * Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori (Kashima dance) Performed during the Kogashi Matsuri at the shrine grounds, Atami Station front, Nagisa Kōen, and Ginza Street. The dancers carry ladles with colored papers symbolizing rice grains, praying for abundant harvest and warding off evil. It’s recognized as a Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property. == Trees == Horuto-no-ki ([[:en:Elaeocarpus sylvestris|Elaeacarpus sylvestris var. ellipticus]]): A unique evergreen species rare to Japan. Characterized by smooth gray bark and leathery leaves, it produces white flowers in July or August. Its leaves turn red before shedding. Two species of this genus grow wild in the warm temperate regions of Japan. Kinomiya no O-kusu (Camphor Tree, Cinnamomum camphora): This colossal tree, standing 23 meters in circumference and estimated to be over 2,000 years old, is recognized as Japan's second largest and oldest kusunoki tree. Known as Goshinboku, or the Holy Tree, it's believed that a Shinto god resides within it. Many believe the tree possesses special powers, granting health, safety, and longevity to those who visit. The bark of this tree is brown and lightly fissured, and its wood is often used in furniture and sculpture. Extracts from the leaves of this tree have medicinal uses in Chinese medicine. It is designated as a natural monument. == Other natural treasures == Beyond the Kinomiya Shrine, other notable trees include Japan's largest camphor tree located at a Hachiman Shrine in Kamo-cho, Kagoshima, and the oldest tree in Japan, a 3,000-year-old kusunoki found in Saga Prefecture. The Kinomiya Shrine is surrounded by a woodland which can be classified as a small laurel forest or ''shoyo-juinrin''. Many trees in this forest are broadleaf evergreens, safeguarding aspects of the local flora from development. == Other == * In May 2011, a 300-year-old holly oak tree next to the torii toppled at its base and damaged the 1920s torii. == Access == * About a 5-minute walk from [[:en:Kinomiya Station|Kinomiya Station]] (JR Itō Line). Also walkable (about 18 minutes) from [[:en:Atami Station|Atami Station]] or reachable by city bus (Ten Nation Pass line or Nishiyama loop) to “Kinomiya Jinja Mae” bus stop.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/praying/access/|title=Access|publisher=Kinomiya Jinja|accessdate=2021-04-21}} The shrine grounds are open from 9:00 to 17:00. == References == * Tanigawa Ken’ichi ed., "Nihon no Kami, Jinja to Seichi Vol.10 Tōkai", Hakusuisha, 1987 == See Also == * Kinomiya faith * Kashima Odori == Notes == === Notes === {{notelist}} === Sources === {{Reflist|2}} == External Links == {{commonscat|Kinomiya-jinja}} * [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/ Official Website of Kinomiya Jinja] * [https://atami.travel/atami-tourism/kinomiya-shrin/ Atami Tourism Bureau - Kinomiya Jinja] * {{Cultural Heritage Online|22_shizuoka|7274|Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property: Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori}} {{Shinto Navbox}} {{Shinto-stub}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{translated page|ja|来宮神社|version=104107598|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 7]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Shizuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:History of Atami]] [[Category:Yamato Takeru]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Son-sha]] [[Category:Atami, Shizuoka]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:everybodywiki import successful]][[Category:everybodywiki import successful]] }} [[Category:Everybody linked]] {{everybodywiki link|Kinomiya Shrine}} [[Category:Yamato Takeru]] [[Category:Buildings in Atami]] [[Category:History of Atami]] [[Category:Son-sha in Shizuoka Prefecture]] {{Commons category|Kinomiya-jinja}} [[ja:来宮神社]] [[zh:來宮神社]] {{wikidata link|Q11523682}}

[[File:Kinomiya jinja - March 7 2021 - various 14 58 24 831000.jpeg|thumb|Torii]] === Position in Atami City === Located in the hilly area near the center of the city, Kinomiya Jinja is considered a central shrine of the Atami area. Its festival, the Kogashi Matsuri (below), is Atami’s largest festival. It also performs rituals for many other shrines in Atami City that do not have their own resident priest. Only Izusan Jinja, Imamiya Jinja, and Ajiko Jinja have their own priests. Other shrines such as Misogino Taki Jinja, Meisui Jinja, Danna Jinja, Fujimori Inari Jinja, Yunomae Jinja, Goten Inari Jinja, Dairokuten-son Jinja, Tagajinja, Shimotaga Jinja, Tsushima Jinja, Koyama Shinmeigū, Wadanoki Jinja, and others are served by Kinomiya Jinja’s priests. Wada Hachiman Jinja’s rites are conducted by Imamiya Jinja’s priest, and Hatsuki Jinja on Hatsushima (an offshore island of Atami) is served by Izusan Jinja’s priest. As Atami’s tourism fortunes waned after the Bubble Economy collapse, pilgrimages to Kinomiya Jinja also declined. However, as Atami tourism recovered in the 2010s, Kinomiya Jinja also saw an increase in visitors. They introduced selfie stands, an open cafe, walking guides, and collaborated with local shops to create new sweets. In 2017, about 688,000 people visited, over four times the roughly 157,000 in 2008.[https://mainichi.jp/articles/20181203/dde/001/040/033000c “Check: Rebound with a Sacred Camphor Tree—Kinomiya Jinja in Atami leverages youth and female appeal”], Mainichi Shimbun (Evening edition), December 3, 2018, p.1. Accessed December 7, 2018. == Main festivals == === Kogashi Matsuri === * festival “Kogashi Matsuri” held around July 15 (including the eve on July 14 and events through July 16). Originally, as old lunar calendar June 15 was the day the fishermen discovered the wooden deity, they held the festival then, but in Meiji times it changed to the solar calendar.[http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/reitaisai.html festival] Kinomiya Jinja official site ** July 14: Eve festival (Yoi-miya-sai), praying for successful ceremonies. ** July 15: festival “Kogashi Matsuri” *** “Miya Mikoshi Togyo” (9:00–15:00): The shrine’s mikoshi visits Atami Station, Shinsui Park, Ginza-chō, and other city areas. *** “Reitaisai Hōhei” (11:00–): Offerings of mugikogashi (roasted barley flour), lily bulbs, bitter oranges, and tokoro jelly according to tradition. *** “Hōshuku Shinnei Gishiki” (11:40–13:00): Kashima Odori (Kashima dance), Miko Kagura (shrine maiden dance), Urayasu no Mai. *** “Kogashi Matsuri Dashi Contest” (18:30–21:30): About 30+ festival floats line up on National Route 135, which is closed off near Hotel Ōnoya through Atami Sun Beach, competing in a parade-style contest. ** July 16: *** “Jinkō-sai” (Shinkō-sai) **** “Hōshuku Shinnei Gishiki” (8:30–): Kashima Odori, Miko Kagura, Urayasu no Mai **** “Goshinkō Gyōretsu” (9:50–15:40): A procession of about 500 people including Tengu-masked, high-geta wearing Sarutahiko distributing mugikogashi (symbolizing rice), a Mikoshi, Shishimai (lion dance), priests, etc. They visit Yunomae Jinja, Atami Station, Sun Beach (with a mikoshi purification), Nagisa Kōen (with dances), and Ginza. At Ginza (in front of Ozawa Himono-ten[http://atamii.jp/today/73259/ Goshinkō parade in Atami city by Kinomiya Jinja concluding festival], Atami Net News, 2017/7/17), Kashima Odori is also performed. **** “Kanchōsai” (15:40–) *** “Kogashi Matsuri Dashi Contest” (18:30–21:00) === Setsubun festival === On Setsubun (February 3), a lively bean-throwing ceremony takes place with participating celebrities. Past participants include: * Izumi Pinko * Ehara Hiroyuki * Kuroda Arthur * Satō Yōko (violinist) * Nishikido Oyakata (former sumo wrestler Mitoizumi Masato) * Hashida Sugako * Hayashi Mariko * Motoki Daisuke == Shrine Buildings == The honden is nagare-zukuri style, connected with heiden and haiden in a gongen-zukuri arrangement. == Subsidiary Shrines == Within the precincts: * Kinomiya Inari-sha (Inari shrine from Fushimi Inari Taisha in Kyoto) * Kinomiya Benzaiten (Benzaiten statue by Takamura Kōun is shown on November 23) * Mitsumine Jinja [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/top/setsumassha.html Kinomiya Jinja – Subsidiary Shrines] (Accessed December 7, 2018) == Cultural Properties == [[File:Azusawake Jinja no Okusu -02.jpg|thumb|150px|Great Camphor Tree of Azusawake Jinja]] === National Natural Monument === {{Main|{{ill|Azusawake Jinja no Ōkusu|ja|阿豆佐和気神社の大クス|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Azusawake Jinja no Ōkusu|qq=|1=Azusawakejinja-no-Okusu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q60403026}}|{{ill|Kamanariya Heishichi|ja|釜鳴屋平七|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamanariya Heishichi|qq=|1=kamanariya heishichi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q65289080}}}} * The Great Camphor Tree of Azusawake Jinja (over 2000 years old, trunk circumference about 24m, height 20m), designated in Shōwa 8. Circling it once is said to extend life by one year or grant wishes. Historically, seven camphor trees stood here, but during the Ansei era (1855–60), a dispute related to fishing rights (the Ōami/maguro-ami incident) forced them to cut five for lawsuit costs.[https://www.city.atami.lg.jp/kosodate/shogaigakushu/1011165/1006016/1009091/1009107.html Episode 14: Local Hero Kamanariya Heishichi] - Atami City Hall[http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/supporting_party/ 50th Anniversary of Iitakeru no Mikoto’s 1300th Enshrinement: Rebuilding Senshūden and Grounds Improvement Project] - Kinomiya Jinja Another large camphor stands near the entrance. === Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property === * Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori (Kashima dance) Performed during the Kogashi Matsuri at the shrine grounds, Atami Station front, Nagisa Kōen, and Ginza Street. The dancers carry ladles with colored papers symbolizing rice grains, praying for abundant harvest and warding off evil. It’s recognized as a Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property. == Trees == Horuto-no-ki ([[:en:Elaeocarpus sylvestris|Elaeacarpus sylvestris var. ellipticus]]): A unique evergreen species rare to Japan. Characterized by smooth gray bark and leathery leaves, it produces white flowers in July or August. Its leaves turn red before shedding. Two species of this genus grow wild in the warm temperate regions of Japan. Kinomiya no O-kusu (Camphor Tree, Cinnamomum camphora): This colossal tree, standing 23 meters in circumference and estimated to be over 2,000 years old, is recognized as Japan's second largest and oldest kusunoki tree. Known as Goshinboku, or the Holy Tree, it's believed that a Shinto god resides within it. Many believe the tree possesses special powers, granting health, safety, and longevity to those who visit. The bark of this tree is brown and lightly fissured, and its wood is often used in furniture and sculpture. Extracts from the leaves of this tree have medicinal uses in Chinese medicine. It is designated as a natural monument. == Other natural treasures == Beyond the Kinomiya Shrine, other notable trees include Japan's largest camphor tree located at a Hachiman Shrine in Kamo-cho, Kagoshima, and the oldest tree in Japan, a 3,000-year-old kusunoki found in Saga Prefecture. The Kinomiya Shrine is surrounded by a woodland which can be classified as a small laurel forest or ''shoyo-juinrin''. Many trees in this forest are broadleaf evergreens, safeguarding aspects of the local flora from development. == Other == * In May 2011, a 300-year-old holly oak tree next to the torii toppled at its base and damaged the 1920s torii. == Access == * About a 5-minute walk from [[:en:Kinomiya Station|Kinomiya Station]] (JR Itō Line). Also walkable (about 18 minutes) from [[:en:Atami Station|Atami Station]] or reachable by city bus (Ten Nation Pass line or Nishiyama loop) to “Kinomiya Jinja Mae” bus stop.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/praying/access/|title=Access|publisher=Kinomiya Jinja|accessdate=2021-04-21}} The shrine grounds are open from 9:00 to 17:00. == References == * Tanigawa Ken’ichi ed., "Nihon no Kami, Jinja to Seichi Vol.10 Tōkai", Hakusuisha, 1987 == See Also == * Kinomiya faith * Kashima Odori == Notes == === Notes === {{notelist}} === Sources === {{Reflist|2}} == External Links == {{commonscat|Kinomiya-jinja}} * [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/ Official Website of Kinomiya Jinja] * [https://atami.travel/atami-tourism/kinomiya-shrin/ Atami Tourism Bureau - Kinomiya Jinja] * {{Cultural Heritage Online|22_shizuoka|7274|Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property: Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori}} {{Shinto Navbox}} {{Shinto-stub}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{translated page|ja|来宮神社|version=104107598|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 7]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Shizuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:History of Atami]] [[Category:Yamato Takeru]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Son-sha]] [[Category:Atami, Shizuoka]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:everybodywiki import successful]][[Category:everybodywiki import successful]] }} [[Category:Everybody linked]] {{everybodywiki link|Kinomiya Shrine}} [[Category:Yamato Takeru]] [[Category:Buildings in Atami]] [[Category:History of Atami]] [[Category:Son-sha in Shizuoka Prefecture]] {{Commons category|Kinomiya-jinja}} [[ja:来宮神社]] [[zh:來宮神社]] {{wikidata link|Q11523682}}

Wadō 3 (710) | honden = Nagare-zukuri style | festival = July 15 | ceremonies = Kogashi Matsuri (July 15–16) }} The [[Kinomiya Shrine]] is located in [[:en:Atami|Atami]], [[:en:Shizuoka (city)|Shizuoka]], and is famous for its natural treasures, especially the historic trees within its grounds.{{Cite web |last=Author |first=No |date=1999-12-08 |title=The natural treasures of Kinomiya Shrine |url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/1999/12/08/environment/the-natural-treasures-of-kinomiya-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-19 |website=The Japan Times |language=en}} It is located near [[:en:Kinomiya Station|Kinomiya Station]],{{Cite web |title=Expand your life expectancy at Kinomiya shrine, in Atami city｜TOMO – 供TOMO 玄米コーヒーオンラインストア |url=https://tomo.life/en/blogs/shinto-and-shrines/lets-visit-kinomiya-shrine |access-date=2023-10-19 |website=tomo.life}} and serves [[Amazake]]. [[File:Cinnamomum camphora 20100612 (Kinomiya Shrine) (B).jpg|thumb|The large camphor tree of Azusawake Jinja]] [[File:Cinnamomum camphora 20100612 (Kinomiya Shrine) (2nd).jpg|thumb|The second large camphor tree]] '''Kinomiya Jinja''' is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in [[:en:Atami|Atami City]], [[:en:Shizuoka Prefecture|Shizuoka Prefecture]], Japan. Under the modern shrine Rank system, it was once a village shrine. == Shrine name == Historically known as “Kimiya Myōjin” or “Kinomiya Daimyōjin,” among others. After the Meiji Restoration, it was identified as the “Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja” (阿豆佐和気命神社) as a result of being associated with a Shikinaisha in that name. Later, when it was found that this was incorrect, it reverted to its current name.{{efn|However, pamphlets distributed by the shrine still state, “It is recorded in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō as ‘Azusawake Jinja.’”}} {{efn|Other candidates for Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja include a shrine of the same name in Toshima Village, Tokyo.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=http://www.tokyo-jinjacho.or.jp/tosho/2843/|title=Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja|publisher=Tokyo Jinja-chō|accessdate=2021-04-21}}}} == Enshrined Deities == * Yamato Takeru no Mikoto * Iitakeru no Mikoto (Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto = Isonotakeru?), identified as the wood (tree) deity Iitakeru (Itsu no Takeri). * Ōnamuchi no Mikoto (Ōkuninushi no Mikoto) In addition, Inari Jinja, Kakimoto-sha, and Tenjin-sha are enshrined in the same hall. The "Sōyuyama Engi (Sōyu-san Engi)" describes this shrine as the “jinushigami” (local guardian deity) of Izusan Jinja. Because “Kinomiya” can be interpreted as “I no Miya” meaning “忌の宮” (taboo shrine), many people come here to pray for abstinence from certain things (such as alcohol). == History == The founding time is unknown. According to shrine tradition, in Wadō 3 (710), fishermen found what seemed to be a divine wooden root caught in their fishing net three times in Atami Bay. They enshrined this root under a pine tree and offered roasted barley flour (mugi-kogashi). That night, Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto appeared in a dream, complaining about the noise of the sea, so they moved the deity to the current location in the forest. Because it was originally a wooden root, the shrine came to be called “Ki no Miya” (Kinomiya). This tradition strongly reflects “Kinomiya faith,” where driftwood or a piece of wood is worshiped, and Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto is revered as a wood (tree) deity. There is also a legend that Sakanoue no Tamuramaro prayed for victory here and enshrined divided spirits of this deity in various places in the Tohoku region. The shrine was a village shrine under the modern shrine system. After World War II, given its history and activities, it was added to the list of Beppyo Shrines under the Association of Shinto Shrines. Also walkable (about 18 minutes) from [[:en:Atami Station|Atami Station]] or reachable by city bus (Ten Nation Pass line or Nishiyama loop) to “Kinomiya Jinja Mae” bus stop.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/praying/access/|title=Access|publisher=Kinomiya Jinja|accessdate=2021-04-21}} The shrine grounds are open from 9:00 to 17:00. == References == * Tanigawa Ken’ichi ed., "Nihon no Kami, Jinja to Seichi Vol.10 Tōkai", Hakusuisha, 1987 == See Also == * Kinomiya faith * Kashima Odori == Notes == === Notes === {{notelist}} === Sources === {{Reflist|2}} == External Links == {{commonscat|Kinomiya-jinja}} * [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/ Official Website of Kinomiya Jinja] * [https://atami.travel/atami-tourism/kinomiya-shrin/ Atami Tourism Bureau - Kinomiya Jinja] * {{Cultural Heritage Online|22_shizuoka|7274|Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property: Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori}} {{Shinto Navbox}} {{Shinto-stub}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{translated page|ja|来宮神社|version=104107598|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 7]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Shizuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:History of Atami]] [[Category:Yamato Takeru]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Son-sha]] [[Category:Atami, Shizuoka]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:everybodywiki import successful]][[Category:everybodywiki import successful]] }} [[Category:Everybody linked]] {{everybodywiki link|Kinomiya Shrine}} [[Category:Yamato Takeru]] [[Category:Buildings in Atami]] [[Category:History of Atami]] [[Category:Son-sha in Shizuoka Prefecture]] {{Commons category|Kinomiya-jinja}} [[ja:来宮神社]] [[zh:來宮神社]] {{wikidata link|Q11523682}}

Wadō 3 (710) | honden = Nagare-zukuri style | festival = July 15 | ceremonies = Kogashi Matsuri (July 15–16) }} The [[Kinomiya Shrine]] is located in [[:en:Atami|Atami]], [[:en:Shizuoka (city)|Shizuoka]], and is famous for its natural treasures, especially the historic trees within its grounds.{{Cite web |last=Author |first=No |date=1999-12-08 |title=The natural treasures of Kinomiya Shrine |url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/1999/12/08/environment/the-natural-treasures-of-kinomiya-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-19 |website=The Japan Times |language=en}} It is located near [[:en:Kinomiya Station|Kinomiya Station]],{{Cite web |title=Expand your life expectancy at Kinomiya shrine, in Atami city｜TOMO – 供TOMO 玄米コーヒーオンラインストア |url=https://tomo.life/en/blogs/shinto-and-shrines/lets-visit-kinomiya-shrine |access-date=2023-10-19 |website=tomo.life}} and serves [[Amazake]]. [[File:Cinnamomum camphora 20100612 (Kinomiya Shrine) (B).jpg|thumb|The large camphor tree of Azusawake Jinja]] [[File:Cinnamomum camphora 20100612 (Kinomiya Shrine) (2nd).jpg|thumb|The second large camphor tree]] '''Kinomiya Jinja''' is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in [[:en:Atami|Atami City]], [[:en:Shizuoka Prefecture|Shizuoka Prefecture]], Japan. Under the modern shrine Rank system, it was once a village shrine. == Shrine name == Historically known as “Kimiya Myōjin” or “Kinomiya Daimyōjin,” among others. After the Meiji Restoration, it was identified as the “Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja” (阿豆佐和気命神社) as a result of being associated with a Shikinaisha in that name. Later, when it was found that this was incorrect, it reverted to its current name.{{efn|However, pamphlets distributed by the shrine still state, “It is recorded in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō as ‘Azusawake Jinja.’”}} {{efn|Other candidates for Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja include a shrine of the same name in Toshima Village, Tokyo.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=http://www.tokyo-jinjacho.or.jp/tosho/2843/|title=Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja|publisher=Tokyo Jinja-chō|accessdate=2021-04-21}}}} == Enshrined Deities == * Yamato Takeru no Mikoto * Iitakeru no Mikoto (Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto = Isonotakeru?), identified as the wood (tree) deity Iitakeru (Itsu no Takeri). * Ōnamuchi no Mikoto (Ōkuninushi no Mikoto) In addition, Inari Jinja, Kakimoto-sha, and Tenjin-sha are enshrined in the same hall. The "Sōyuyama Engi (Sōyu-san Engi)" describes this shrine as the “jinushigami” (local guardian deity) of Izusan Jinja. Because “Kinomiya” can be interpreted as “I no Miya” meaning “忌の宮” (taboo shrine), many people come here to pray for abstinence from certain things (such as alcohol). == History == The founding time is unknown. According to shrine tradition, in Wadō 3 (710), fishermen found what seemed to be a divine wooden root caught in their fishing net three times in Atami Bay. They enshrined this root under a pine tree and offered roasted barley flour (mugi-kogashi). That night, Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto appeared in a dream, complaining about the noise of the sea, so they moved the deity to the current location in the forest. Because it was originally a wooden root, the shrine came to be called “Ki no Miya” (Kinomiya). This tradition strongly reflects “Kinomiya faith,” where driftwood or a piece of wood is worshiped, and Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto is revered as a wood (tree) deity. There is also a legend that Sakanoue no Tamuramaro prayed for victory here and enshrined divided spirits of this deity in various places in the Tohoku region. The shrine was a village shrine under the modern shrine system. After World War II, given its history and activities, it was added to the list of Beppyo Shrines under the Association of Shinto Shrines. [[File:Kinomiya jinja - March 7 2021 - various 14 58 24 831000.jpeg|thumb|Torii]] === Position in Atami City === Located in the hilly area near the center of the city, Kinomiya Jinja is considered a central shrine of the Atami area. Its festival, the Kogashi Matsuri (below), is Atami’s largest festival. It also performs rituals for many other shrines in Atami City that do not have their own resident priest. Only Izusan Jinja, Imamiya Jinja, and Ajiko Jinja have their own priests. Other shrines such as Misogino Taki Jinja, Meisui Jinja, Danna Jinja, Fujimori Inari Jinja, Yunomae Jinja, Goten Inari Jinja, Dairokuten-son Jinja, Tagajinja, Shimotaga Jinja, Tsushima Jinja, Koyama Shinmeigū, Wadanoki Jinja, and others are served by Kinomiya Jinja’s priests. Wada Hachiman Jinja’s rites are conducted by Imamiya Jinja’s priest, and Hatsuki Jinja on Hatsushima (an offshore island of Atami) is served by Izusan Jinja’s priest. As Atami’s tourism fortunes waned after the Bubble Economy collapse, pilgrimages to Kinomiya Jinja also declined. However, as Atami tourism recovered in the 2010s, Kinomiya Jinja also saw an increase in visitors. They introduced selfie stands, an open cafe, walking guides, and collaborated with local shops to create new sweets. In 2017, about 688,000 people visited, over four times the roughly 157,000 in 2008.[https://mainichi.jp/articles/20181203/dde/001/040/033000c “Check: Rebound with a Sacred Camphor Tree—Kinomiya Jinja in Atami leverages youth and female appeal”], Mainichi Shimbun (Evening edition), December 3, 2018, p.1. Accessed December 7, 2018. == Main festivals == === Kogashi Matsuri === * festival “Kogashi Matsuri” held around July 15 (including the eve on July 14 and events through July 16). Originally, as old lunar calendar June 15 was the day the fishermen discovered the wooden deity, they held the festival then, but in Meiji times it changed to the solar calendar.[http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/reitaisai.html festival] Kinomiya Jinja official site ** July 14: Eve festival (Yoi-miya-sai), praying for successful ceremonies. ** July 15: festival “Kogashi Matsuri” *** “Miya Mikoshi Togyo” (9:00–15:00): The shrine’s mikoshi visits Atami Station, Shinsui Park, Ginza-chō, and other city areas. *** “Reitaisai Hōhei” (11:00–): Offerings of mugikogashi (roasted barley flour), lily bulbs, bitter oranges, and tokoro jelly according to tradition. *** “Hōshuku Shinnei Gishiki” (11:40–13:00): Kashima Odori (Kashima dance), Miko Kagura (shrine maiden dance), Urayasu no Mai. *** “Kogashi Matsuri Dashi Contest” (18:30–21:30): About 30+ festival floats line up on National Route 135, which is closed off near Hotel Ōnoya through Atami Sun Beach, competing in a parade-style contest. ** July 16: *** “Jinkō-sai” (Shinkō-sai) **** “Hōshuku Shinnei Gishiki” (8:30–): Kashima Odori, Miko Kagura, Urayasu no Mai **** “Goshinkō Gyōretsu” (9:50–15:40): A procession of about 500 people including Tengu-masked, high-geta wearing Sarutahiko distributing mugikogashi (symbolizing rice), a Mikoshi, Shishimai (lion dance), priests, etc. They visit Yunomae Jinja, Atami Station, Sun Beach (with a mikoshi purification), Nagisa Kōen (with dances), and Ginza. At Ginza (in front of Ozawa Himono-ten[http://atamii.jp/today/73259/ Goshinkō parade in Atami city by Kinomiya Jinja concluding festival], Atami Net News, 2017/7/17), Kashima Odori is also performed. **** “Kanchōsai” (15:40–) *** “Kogashi Matsuri Dashi Contest” (18:30–21:00) === Setsubun festival === On Setsubun (February 3), a lively bean-throwing ceremony takes place with participating celebrities. Past participants include: * Izumi Pinko * Ehara Hiroyuki * Kuroda Arthur * Satō Yōko (violinist) * Nishikido Oyakata (former sumo wrestler Mitoizumi Masato) * Hashida Sugako * Hayashi Mariko * Motoki Daisuke == Shrine Buildings == The honden is nagare-zukuri style, connected with heiden and haiden in a gongen-zukuri arrangement. == Subsidiary Shrines == Within the precincts: * Kinomiya Inari-sha (Inari shrine from Fushimi Inari Taisha in Kyoto) * Kinomiya Benzaiten (Benzaiten statue by Takamura Kōun is shown on November 23) * Mitsumine Jinja [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/top/setsumassha.html Kinomiya Jinja – Subsidiary Shrines] (Accessed December 7, 2018) == Cultural Properties == [[File:Azusawake Jinja no Okusu -02.jpg|thumb|150px|Great Camphor Tree of Azusawake Jinja]] === National Natural Monument === {{Main|{{ill|Azusawake Jinja no Ōkusu|ja|阿豆佐和気神社の大クス|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Azusawake Jinja no Ōkusu|qq=|1=Azusawakejinja-no-Okusu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q60403026}}|{{ill|Kamanariya Heishichi|ja|釜鳴屋平七|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamanariya Heishichi|qq=|1=kamanariya heishichi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q65289080}}}} * The Great Camphor Tree of Azusawake Jinja (over 2000 years old, trunk circumference about 24m, height 20m), designated in Shōwa 8. Circling it once is said to extend life by one year or grant wishes. Historically, seven camphor trees stood here, but during the Ansei era (1855–60), a dispute related to fishing rights (the Ōami/maguro-ami incident) forced them to cut five for lawsuit costs.[https://www.city.atami.lg.jp/kosodate/shogaigakushu/1011165/1006016/1009091/1009107.html Episode 14: Local Hero Kamanariya Heishichi] - Atami City Hall[http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/supporting_party/ 50th Anniversary of Iitakeru no Mikoto’s 1300th Enshrinement: Rebuilding Senshūden and Grounds Improvement Project] - Kinomiya Jinja Another large camphor stands near the entrance. === Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property === * Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori (Kashima dance) Performed during the Kogashi Matsuri at the shrine grounds, Atami Station front, Nagisa Kōen, and Ginza Street. The dancers carry ladles with colored papers symbolizing rice grains, praying for abundant harvest and warding off evil. It’s recognized as a Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property. == Trees == Horuto-no-ki ([[:en:Elaeocarpus sylvestris|Elaeacarpus sylvestris var. ellipticus]]): A unique evergreen species rare to Japan. Characterized by smooth gray bark and leathery leaves, it produces white flowers in July or August. Its leaves turn red before shedding. Two species of this genus grow wild in the warm temperate regions of Japan. Kinomiya no O-kusu (Camphor Tree, Cinnamomum camphora): This colossal tree, standing 23 meters in circumference and estimated to be over 2,000 years old, is recognized as Japan's second largest and oldest kusunoki tree. Known as Goshinboku, or the Holy Tree, it's believed that a Shinto god resides within it. Many believe the tree possesses special powers, granting health, safety, and longevity to those who visit. The bark of this tree is brown and lightly fissured, and its wood is often used in furniture and sculpture. Extracts from the leaves of this tree have medicinal uses in Chinese medicine. It is designated as a natural monument. == Other natural treasures == Beyond the Kinomiya Shrine, other notable trees include Japan's largest camphor tree located at a Hachiman Shrine in Kamo-cho, Kagoshima, and the oldest tree in Japan, a 3,000-year-old kusunoki found in Saga Prefecture. The Kinomiya Shrine is surrounded by a woodland which can be classified as a small laurel forest or ''shoyo-juinrin''. Many trees in this forest are broadleaf evergreens, safeguarding aspects of the local flora from development. == Other == * In May 2011, a 300-year-old holly oak tree next to the torii toppled at its base and damaged the 1920s torii. == Access == * About a 5-minute walk from [[:en:Kinomiya Station|Kinomiya Station]] (JR Itō Line). Also walkable (about 18 minutes) from [[:en:Atami Station|Atami Station]] or reachable by city bus (Ten Nation Pass line or Nishiyama loop) to “Kinomiya Jinja Mae” bus stop.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/praying/access/|title=Access|publisher=Kinomiya Jinja|accessdate=2021-04-21}} The shrine grounds are open from 9:00 to 17:00. == References == * Tanigawa Ken’ichi ed., "Nihon no Kami, Jinja to Seichi Vol.10 Tōkai", Hakusuisha, 1987 == See Also == * Kinomiya faith * Kashima Odori == Notes == === Notes === {{notelist}} === Sources === {{Reflist|2}} == External Links == {{commonscat|Kinomiya-jinja}} * [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/ Official Website of Kinomiya Jinja] * [https://atami.travel/atami-tourism/kinomiya-shrin/ Atami Tourism Bureau - Kinomiya Jinja] * {{Cultural Heritage Online|22_shizuoka|7274|Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property: Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori}} {{Shinto Navbox}} {{Shinto-stub}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{translated page|ja|来宮神社|version=104107598|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 7]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Shizuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:History of Atami]] [[Category:Yamato Takeru]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Son-sha]] [[Category:Atami, Shizuoka]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:everybodywiki import successful]][[Category:everybodywiki import successful]] }} [[Category:Everybody linked]] {{everybodywiki link|Kinomiya Shrine}} [[Category:Yamato Takeru]] [[Category:Buildings in Atami]] [[Category:History of Atami]] [[Category:Son-sha in Shizuoka Prefecture]] {{Commons category|Kinomiya-jinja}} [[ja:来宮神社]] [[zh:來宮神社]] {{wikidata link|Q11523682}}

[[File:Kinomiya jinja - March 7 2021 - various 14 58 24 831000.jpeg|thumb|Torii]] === Position in Atami City === Located in the hilly area near the center of the city, Kinomiya Jinja is considered a central shrine of the Atami area. Its festival, the Kogashi Matsuri (below), is Atami’s largest festival. It also performs rituals for many other shrines in Atami City that do not have their own resident priest. Only Izusan Jinja, Imamiya Jinja, and Ajiko Jinja have their own priests. Other shrines such as Misogino Taki Jinja, Meisui Jinja, Danna Jinja, Fujimori Inari Jinja, Yunomae Jinja, Goten Inari Jinja, Dairokuten-son Jinja, Tagajinja, Shimotaga Jinja, Tsushima Jinja, Koyama Shinmeigū, Wadanoki Jinja, and others are served by Kinomiya Jinja’s priests. Wada Hachiman Jinja’s rites are conducted by Imamiya Jinja’s priest, and Hatsuki Jinja on Hatsushima (an offshore island of Atami) is served by Izusan Jinja’s priest. As Atami’s tourism fortunes waned after the Bubble Economy collapse, pilgrimages to Kinomiya Jinja also declined. However, as Atami tourism recovered in the 2010s, Kinomiya Jinja also saw an increase in visitors. They introduced selfie stands, an open cafe, walking guides, and collaborated with local shops to create new sweets. In 2017, about 688,000 people visited, over four times the roughly 157,000 in 2008.[https://mainichi.jp/articles/20181203/dde/001/040/033000c “Check: Rebound with a Sacred Camphor Tree—Kinomiya Jinja in Atami leverages youth and female appeal”], Mainichi Shimbun (Evening edition), December 3, 2018, p.1. Accessed December 7, 2018. == Main festivals == === Kogashi Matsuri === * festival “Kogashi Matsuri” held around July 15 (including the eve on July 14 and events through July 16). Originally, as old lunar calendar June 15 was the day the fishermen discovered the wooden deity, they held the festival then, but in Meiji times it changed to the solar calendar.[http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/reitaisai.html festival] Kinomiya Jinja official site ** July 14: Eve festival (Yoi-miya-sai), praying for successful ceremonies. ** July 15: festival “Kogashi Matsuri” *** “Miya Mikoshi Togyo” (9:00–15:00): The shrine’s mikoshi visits Atami Station, Shinsui Park, Ginza-chō, and other city areas. *** “Reitaisai Hōhei” (11:00–): Offerings of mugikogashi (roasted barley flour), lily bulbs, bitter oranges, and tokoro jelly according to tradition. *** “Hōshuku Shinnei Gishiki” (11:40–13:00): Kashima Odori (Kashima dance), Miko Kagura (shrine maiden dance), Urayasu no Mai. *** “Kogashi Matsuri Dashi Contest” (18:30–21:30): About 30+ festival floats line up on National Route 135, which is closed off near Hotel Ōnoya through Atami Sun Beach, competing in a parade-style contest. ** July 16: *** “Jinkō-sai” (Shinkō-sai) **** “Hōshuku Shinnei Gishiki” (8:30–): Kashima Odori, Miko Kagura, Urayasu no Mai **** “Goshinkō Gyōretsu” (9:50–15:40): A procession of about 500 people including Tengu-masked, high-geta wearing Sarutahiko distributing mugikogashi (symbolizing rice), a Mikoshi, Shishimai (lion dance), priests, etc. They visit Yunomae Jinja, Atami Station, Sun Beach (with a mikoshi purification), Nagisa Kōen (with dances), and Ginza. At Ginza (in front of Ozawa Himono-ten[http://atamii.jp/today/73259/ Goshinkō parade in Atami city by Kinomiya Jinja concluding festival], Atami Net News, 2017/7/17), Kashima Odori is also performed. **** “Kanchōsai” (15:40–) *** “Kogashi Matsuri Dashi Contest” (18:30–21:00) === Setsubun festival === On Setsubun (February 3), a lively bean-throwing ceremony takes place with participating celebrities. Past participants include: * Izumi Pinko * Ehara Hiroyuki * Kuroda Arthur * Satō Yōko (violinist) * Nishikido Oyakata (former sumo wrestler Mitoizumi Masato) * Hashida Sugako * Hayashi Mariko * Motoki Daisuke == Shrine Buildings == The honden is nagare-zukuri style, connected with heiden and haiden in a gongen-zukuri arrangement. == Subsidiary Shrines == Within the precincts: * Kinomiya Inari-sha (Inari shrine from Fushimi Inari Taisha in Kyoto) * Kinomiya Benzaiten (Benzaiten statue by Takamura Kōun is shown on November 23) * Mitsumine Jinja [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/top/setsumassha.html Kinomiya Jinja – Subsidiary Shrines] (Accessed December 7, 2018) == Cultural Properties == [[File:Azusawake Jinja no Okusu -02.jpg|thumb|150px|Great Camphor Tree of Azusawake Jinja]] === National Natural Monument === {{Main|{{ill|Azusawake Jinja no Ōkusu|ja|阿豆佐和気神社の大クス|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Azusawake Jinja no Ōkusu|qq=|1=Azusawakejinja-no-Okusu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q60403026}}|{{ill|Kamanariya Heishichi|ja|釜鳴屋平七|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamanariya Heishichi|qq=|1=kamanariya heishichi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q65289080}}}} * The Great Camphor Tree of Azusawake Jinja (over 2000 years old, trunk circumference about 24m, height 20m), designated in Shōwa 8. Circling it once is said to extend life by one year or grant wishes. Historically, seven camphor trees stood here, but during the Ansei era (1855–60), a dispute related to fishing rights (the Ōami/maguro-ami incident) forced them to cut five for lawsuit costs.[https://www.city.atami.lg.jp/kosodate/shogaigakushu/1011165/1006016/1009091/1009107.html Episode 14: Local Hero Kamanariya Heishichi] - Atami City Hall[http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/supporting_party/ 50th Anniversary of Iitakeru no Mikoto’s 1300th Enshrinement: Rebuilding Senshūden and Grounds Improvement Project] - Kinomiya Jinja Another large camphor stands near the entrance. === Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property === * Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori (Kashima dance) Performed during the Kogashi Matsuri at the shrine grounds, Atami Station front, Nagisa Kōen, and Ginza Street. The dancers carry ladles with colored papers symbolizing rice grains, praying for abundant harvest and warding off evil. It’s recognized as a Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property. == Trees == Horuto-no-ki ([[:en:Elaeocarpus sylvestris|Elaeacarpus sylvestris var. ellipticus]]): A unique evergreen species rare to Japan. Characterized by smooth gray bark and leathery leaves, it produces white flowers in July or August. Its leaves turn red before shedding. Two species of this genus grow wild in the warm temperate regions of Japan. Kinomiya no O-kusu (Camphor Tree, Cinnamomum camphora): This colossal tree, standing 23 meters in circumference and estimated to be over 2,000 years old, is recognized as Japan's second largest and oldest kusunoki tree. Known as Goshinboku, or the Holy Tree, it's believed that a Shinto god resides within it. Many believe the tree possesses special powers, granting health, safety, and longevity to those who visit. The bark of this tree is brown and lightly fissured, and its wood is often used in furniture and sculpture. Extracts from the leaves of this tree have medicinal uses in Chinese medicine. It is designated as a natural monument. == Other natural treasures == Beyond the Kinomiya Shrine, other notable trees include Japan's largest camphor tree located at a Hachiman Shrine in Kamo-cho, Kagoshima, and the oldest tree in Japan, a 3,000-year-old kusunoki found in Saga Prefecture. The Kinomiya Shrine is surrounded by a woodland which can be classified as a small laurel forest or ''shoyo-juinrin''. Many trees in this forest are broadleaf evergreens, safeguarding aspects of the local flora from development. == Other == * In May 2011, a 300-year-old holly oak tree next to the torii toppled at its base and damaged the 1920s torii. == Access == * About a 5-minute walk from [[:en:Kinomiya Station|Kinomiya Station]] (JR Itō Line). Also walkable (about 18 minutes) from [[:en:Atami Station|Atami Station]] or reachable by city bus (Ten Nation Pass line or Nishiyama loop) to “Kinomiya Jinja Mae” bus stop.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/praying/access/|title=Access|publisher=Kinomiya Jinja|accessdate=2021-04-21}} The shrine grounds are open from 9:00 to 17:00. == References == * Tanigawa Ken’ichi ed., "Nihon no Kami, Jinja to Seichi Vol.10 Tōkai", Hakusuisha, 1987 == See Also == * Kinomiya faith * Kashima Odori == Notes == === Notes === {{notelist}} === Sources === {{Reflist|2}} == External Links == {{commonscat|Kinomiya-jinja}} * [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/ Official Website of Kinomiya Jinja] * [https://atami.travel/atami-tourism/kinomiya-shrin/ Atami Tourism Bureau - Kinomiya Jinja] * {{Cultural Heritage Online|22_shizuoka|7274|Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property: Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori}} {{Shinto Navbox}} {{Shinto-stub}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{translated page|ja|来宮神社|version=104107598|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 7]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Shizuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:History of Atami]] [[Category:Yamato Takeru]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Son-sha]] [[Category:Atami, Shizuoka]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:everybodywiki import successful]][[Category:everybodywiki import successful]] }} [[Category:Everybody linked]] {{everybodywiki link|Kinomiya Shrine}} [[Category:Yamato Takeru]] [[Category:Buildings in Atami]] [[Category:History of Atami]] [[Category:Son-sha in Shizuoka Prefecture]] {{Commons category|Kinomiya-jinja}} [[ja:来宮神社]] [[zh:來宮神社]] {{wikidata link|Q11523682}}

Wadō 3 (710) | honden = Nagare-zukuri style | festival = July 15 | ceremonies = Kogashi Matsuri (July 15–16) }} The [[Kinomiya Shrine]] is located in [[:en:Atami|Atami]], [[:en:Shizuoka (city)|Shizuoka]], and is famous for its natural treasures, especially the historic trees within its grounds.{{Cite web |last=Author |first=No |date=1999-12-08 |title=The natural treasures of Kinomiya Shrine |url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/1999/12/08/environment/the-natural-treasures-of-kinomiya-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-19 |website=The Japan Times |language=en}} It is located near [[:en:Kinomiya Station|Kinomiya Station]],{{Cite web |title=Expand your life expectancy at Kinomiya shrine, in Atami city｜TOMO – 供TOMO 玄米コーヒーオンラインストア |url=https://tomo.life/en/blogs/shinto-and-shrines/lets-visit-kinomiya-shrine |access-date=2023-10-19 |website=tomo.life}} and serves [[Amazake]]. [[File:Cinnamomum camphora 20100612 (Kinomiya Shrine) (B).jpg|thumb|The large camphor tree of Azusawake Jinja]] [[File:Cinnamomum camphora 20100612 (Kinomiya Shrine) (2nd).jpg|thumb|The second large camphor tree]] '''Kinomiya Jinja''' is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in [[:en:Atami|Atami City]], [[:en:Shizuoka Prefecture|Shizuoka Prefecture]], Japan. Under the modern shrine Rank system, it was once a village shrine. == Shrine name == Historically known as “Kimiya Myōjin” or “Kinomiya Daimyōjin,” among others. After the Meiji Restoration, it was identified as the “Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja” (阿豆佐和気命神社) as a result of being associated with a Shikinaisha in that name. Later, when it was found that this was incorrect, it reverted to its current name.{{efn|However, pamphlets distributed by the shrine still state, “It is recorded in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō as ‘Azusawake Jinja.’”}} {{efn|Other candidates for Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja include a shrine of the same name in Toshima Village, Tokyo.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=http://www.tokyo-jinjacho.or.jp/tosho/2843/|title=Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja|publisher=Tokyo Jinja-chō|accessdate=2021-04-21}}}} == Enshrined Deities == * Yamato Takeru no Mikoto * Iitakeru no Mikoto (Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto = Isonotakeru?), identified as the wood (tree) deity Iitakeru (Itsu no Takeri). * Ōnamuchi no Mikoto (Ōkuninushi no Mikoto) In addition, Inari Jinja, Kakimoto-sha, and Tenjin-sha are enshrined in the same hall. The "Sōyuyama Engi (Sōyu-san Engi)" describes this shrine as the “jinushigami” (local guardian deity) of Izusan Jinja. Because “Kinomiya” can be interpreted as “I no Miya” meaning “忌の宮” (taboo shrine), many people come here to pray for abstinence from certain things (such as alcohol). == History == The founding time is unknown. According to shrine tradition, in Wadō 3 (710), fishermen found what seemed to be a divine wooden root caught in their fishing net three times in Atami Bay. They enshrined this root under a pine tree and offered roasted barley flour (mugi-kogashi). That night, Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto appeared in a dream, complaining about the noise of the sea, so they moved the deity to the current location in the forest. Because it was originally a wooden root, the shrine came to be called “Ki no Miya” (Kinomiya). This tradition strongly reflects “Kinomiya faith,” where driftwood or a piece of wood is worshiped, and Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto is revered as a wood (tree) deity. There is also a legend that Sakanoue no Tamuramaro prayed for victory here and enshrined divided spirits of this deity in various places in the Tohoku region. The shrine was a village shrine under the modern shrine system. After World War II, given its history and activities, it was added to the list of Beppyo Shrines under the Association of Shinto Shrines. Wadō 3 (710) | honden = Nagare-zukuri style | festival = July 15 | ceremonies = Kogashi Matsuri (July 15–16) }} The [[Kinomiya Shrine]] is located in [[:en:Atami|Atami]], [[:en:Shizuoka (city)|Shizuoka]], and is famous for its natural treasures, especially the historic trees within its grounds.{{Cite web |last=Author |first=No |date=1999-12-08 |title=The natural treasures of Kinomiya Shrine |url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/1999/12/08/environment/the-natural-treasures-of-kinomiya-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-19 |website=The Japan Times |language=en}} It is located near [[:en:Kinomiya Station|Kinomiya Station]],{{Cite web |title=Expand your life expectancy at Kinomiya shrine, in Atami city｜TOMO – 供TOMO 玄米コーヒーオンラインストア |url=https://tomo.life/en/blogs/shinto-and-shrines/lets-visit-kinomiya-shrine |access-date=2023-10-19 |website=tomo.life}} and serves [[Amazake]]. [[File:Cinnamomum camphora 20100612 (Kinomiya Shrine) (B).jpg|thumb|The large camphor tree of Azusawake Jinja]] [[File:Cinnamomum camphora 20100612 (Kinomiya Shrine) (2nd).jpg|thumb|The second large camphor tree]] '''Kinomiya Jinja''' is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in [[:en:Atami|Atami City]], [[:en:Shizuoka Prefecture|Shizuoka Prefecture]], Japan. Under the modern shrine Rank system, it was once a village shrine. == Shrine name == Historically known as “Kimiya Myōjin” or “Kinomiya Daimyōjin,” among others. After the Meiji Restoration, it was identified as the “Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja” (阿豆佐和気命神社) as a result of being associated with a Shikinaisha in that name. Later, when it was found that this was incorrect, it reverted to its current name.{{efn|However, pamphlets distributed by the shrine still state, “It is recorded in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō as ‘Azusawake Jinja.’”}} {{efn|Other candidates for Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja include a shrine of the same name in Toshima Village, Tokyo.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=http://www.tokyo-jinjacho.or.jp/tosho/2843/|title=Azusawake no Mikoto Jinja|publisher=Tokyo Jinja-chō|accessdate=2021-04-21}}}} == Enshrined Deities == * Yamato Takeru no Mikoto * Iitakeru no Mikoto (Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto = Isonotakeru?), identified as the wood (tree) deity Iitakeru (Itsu no Takeri). * Ōnamuchi no Mikoto (Ōkuninushi no Mikoto) In addition, Inari Jinja, Kakimoto-sha, and Tenjin-sha are enshrined in the same hall. The "Sōyuyama Engi (Sōyu-san Engi)" describes this shrine as the “jinushigami” (local guardian deity) of Izusan Jinja. Because “Kinomiya” can be interpreted as “I no Miya” meaning “忌の宮” (taboo shrine), many people come here to pray for abstinence from certain things (such as alcohol). == History == The founding time is unknown. According to shrine tradition, in Wadō 3 (710), fishermen found what seemed to be a divine wooden root caught in their fishing net three times in Atami Bay. They enshrined this root under a pine tree and offered roasted barley flour (mugi-kogashi). That night, Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto appeared in a dream, complaining about the noise of the sea, so they moved the deity to the current location in the forest. Because it was originally a wooden root, the shrine came to be called “Ki no Miya” (Kinomiya). This tradition strongly reflects “Kinomiya faith,” where driftwood or a piece of wood is worshiped, and Itsuno Takeri no Mikoto is revered as a wood (tree) deity. There is also a legend that Sakanoue no Tamuramaro prayed for victory here and enshrined divided spirits of this deity in various places in the Tohoku region. The shrine was a village shrine under the modern shrine system. After World War II, given its history and activities, it was added to the list of Beppyo Shrines under the Association of Shinto Shrines. [[File:Kinomiya jinja - March 7 2021 - various 14 58 24 831000.jpeg|thumb|Torii]] === Position in Atami City === Located in the hilly area near the center of the city, Kinomiya Jinja is considered a central shrine of the Atami area. Its festival, the Kogashi Matsuri (below), is Atami’s largest festival. It also performs rituals for many other shrines in Atami City that do not have their own resident priest. Only Izusan Jinja, Imamiya Jinja, and Ajiko Jinja have their own priests. Other shrines such as Misogino Taki Jinja, Meisui Jinja, Danna Jinja, Fujimori Inari Jinja, Yunomae Jinja, Goten Inari Jinja, Dairokuten-son Jinja, Tagajinja, Shimotaga Jinja, Tsushima Jinja, Koyama Shinmeigū, Wadanoki Jinja, and others are served by Kinomiya Jinja’s priests. Wada Hachiman Jinja’s rites are conducted by Imamiya Jinja’s priest, and Hatsuki Jinja on Hatsushima (an offshore island of Atami) is served by Izusan Jinja’s priest. As Atami’s tourism fortunes waned after the Bubble Economy collapse, pilgrimages to Kinomiya Jinja also declined. However, as Atami tourism recovered in the 2010s, Kinomiya Jinja also saw an increase in visitors. They introduced selfie stands, an open cafe, walking guides, and collaborated with local shops to create new sweets. In 2017, about 688,000 people visited, over four times the roughly 157,000 in 2008.[https://mainichi.jp/articles/20181203/dde/001/040/033000c “Check: Rebound with a Sacred Camphor Tree—Kinomiya Jinja in Atami leverages youth and female appeal”], Mainichi Shimbun (Evening edition), December 3, 2018, p.1. Accessed December 7, 2018. == Main festivals == === Kogashi Matsuri === * festival “Kogashi Matsuri” held around July 15 (including the eve on July 14 and events through July 16). Originally, as old lunar calendar June 15 was the day the fishermen discovered the wooden deity, they held the festival then, but in Meiji times it changed to the solar calendar.[http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/reitaisai.html festival] Kinomiya Jinja official site ** July 14: Eve festival (Yoi-miya-sai), praying for successful ceremonies. ** July 15: festival “Kogashi Matsuri” *** “Miya Mikoshi Togyo” (9:00–15:00): The shrine’s mikoshi visits Atami Station, Shinsui Park, Ginza-chō, and other city areas. *** “Reitaisai Hōhei” (11:00–): Offerings of mugikogashi (roasted barley flour), lily bulbs, bitter oranges, and tokoro jelly according to tradition. *** “Hōshuku Shinnei Gishiki” (11:40–13:00): Kashima Odori (Kashima dance), Miko Kagura (shrine maiden dance), Urayasu no Mai. *** “Kogashi Matsuri Dashi Contest” (18:30–21:30): About 30+ festival floats line up on National Route 135, which is closed off near Hotel Ōnoya through Atami Sun Beach, competing in a parade-style contest. ** July 16: *** “Jinkō-sai” (Shinkō-sai) **** “Hōshuku Shinnei Gishiki” (8:30–): Kashima Odori, Miko Kagura, Urayasu no Mai **** “Goshinkō Gyōretsu” (9:50–15:40): A procession of about 500 people including Tengu-masked, high-geta wearing Sarutahiko distributing mugikogashi (symbolizing rice), a Mikoshi, Shishimai (lion dance), priests, etc. They visit Yunomae Jinja, Atami Station, Sun Beach (with a mikoshi purification), Nagisa Kōen (with dances), and Ginza. At Ginza (in front of Ozawa Himono-ten[http://atamii.jp/today/73259/ Goshinkō parade in Atami city by Kinomiya Jinja concluding festival], Atami Net News, 2017/7/17), Kashima Odori is also performed. **** “Kanchōsai” (15:40–) *** “Kogashi Matsuri Dashi Contest” (18:30–21:00) === Setsubun festival === On Setsubun (February 3), a lively bean-throwing ceremony takes place with participating celebrities. Past participants include: * Izumi Pinko * Ehara Hiroyuki * Kuroda Arthur * Satō Yōko (violinist) * Nishikido Oyakata (former sumo wrestler Mitoizumi Masato) * Hashida Sugako * Hayashi Mariko * Motoki Daisuke == Shrine Buildings == The honden is nagare-zukuri style, connected with heiden and haiden in a gongen-zukuri arrangement. == Subsidiary Shrines == Within the precincts: * Kinomiya Inari-sha (Inari shrine from Fushimi Inari Taisha in Kyoto) * Kinomiya Benzaiten (Benzaiten statue by Takamura Kōun is shown on November 23) * Mitsumine Jinja [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/top/setsumassha.html Kinomiya Jinja – Subsidiary Shrines] (Accessed December 7, 2018) == Cultural Properties == [[File:Azusawake Jinja no Okusu -02.jpg|thumb|150px|Great Camphor Tree of Azusawake Jinja]] === National Natural Monument === {{Main|{{ill|Azusawake Jinja no Ōkusu|ja|阿豆佐和気神社の大クス|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Azusawake Jinja no Ōkusu|1=Azusawakejinja-no-Okusu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q60403026}}|{{ill|Kamanariya Heishichi|ja|釜鳴屋平七|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamanariya Heishichi|1=kamanariya heishichi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q65289080}}}} * The Great Camphor Tree of Azusawake Jinja (over 2000 years old, trunk circumference about 24m, height 20m), designated in Shōwa 8. Circling it once is said to extend life by one year or grant wishes. Historically, seven camphor trees stood here, but during the Ansei era (1855–60), a dispute related to fishing rights (the Ōami/maguro-ami incident) forced them to cut five for lawsuit costs.[https://www.city.atami.lg.jp/kosodate/shogaigakushu/1011165/1006016/1009091/1009107.html Episode 14: Local Hero Kamanariya Heishichi] - Atami City Hall[http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/supporting_party/ 50th Anniversary of Iitakeru no Mikoto’s 1300th Enshrinement: Rebuilding Senshūden and Grounds Improvement Project] - Kinomiya Jinja Another large camphor stands near the entrance. === Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property === * Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori (Kashima dance) Performed during the Kogashi Matsuri at the shrine grounds, Atami Station front, Nagisa Kōen, and Ginza Street. The dancers carry ladles with colored papers symbolizing rice grains, praying for abundant harvest and warding off evil. It’s recognized as a Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property. == Trees == Horuto-no-ki ([[:en:Elaeocarpus sylvestris|Elaeacarpus sylvestris var. ellipticus]]): A unique evergreen species rare to Japan. Characterized by smooth gray bark and leathery leaves, it produces white flowers in July or August. Its leaves turn red before shedding. Two species of this genus grow wild in the warm temperate regions of Japan. Kinomiya no O-kusu (Camphor Tree, Cinnamomum camphora): This colossal tree, standing 23 meters in circumference and estimated to be over 2,000 years old, is recognized as Japan's second largest and oldest kusunoki tree. Known as Goshinboku, or the Holy Tree, it's believed that a Shinto god resides within it. Many believe the tree possesses special powers, granting health, safety, and longevity to those who visit. The bark of this tree is brown and lightly fissured, and its wood is often used in furniture and sculpture. Extracts from the leaves of this tree have medicinal uses in Chinese medicine. It is designated as a natural monument. == Other natural treasures == Beyond the Kinomiya Shrine, other notable trees include Japan's largest camphor tree located at a Hachiman Shrine in Kamo-cho, Kagoshima, and the oldest tree in Japan, a 3,000-year-old kusunoki found in Saga Prefecture. The Kinomiya Shrine is surrounded by a woodland which can be classified as a small laurel forest or ''shoyo-juinrin''. Many trees in this forest are broadleaf evergreens, safeguarding aspects of the local flora from development. == Other == * In May 2011, a 300-year-old holly oak tree next to the torii toppled at its base and damaged the 1920s torii. == Access == * About a 5-minute walk from [[:en:Kinomiya Station|Kinomiya Station]] (JR Itō Line). Also walkable (about 18 minutes) from [[:en:Atami Station|Atami Station]] or reachable by city bus (Ten Nation Pass line or Nishiyama loop) to “Kinomiya Jinja Mae” bus stop.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/praying/access/|title=Access|publisher=Kinomiya Jinja|accessdate=2021-04-21}} The shrine grounds are open from 9:00 to 17:00. == References == * Tanigawa Ken’ichi ed., "Nihon no Kami, Jinja to Seichi Vol.10 Tōkai", Hakusuisha, 1987 == See Also == * Kinomiya faith * Kashima Odori == Notes == === Notes === {{notelist}} === Sources === {{Reflist|2}} == External Links == {{commonscat|Kinomiya-jinja}} * [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/ Official Website of Kinomiya Jinja] * [https://atami.travel/atami-tourism/kinomiya-shrin/ Atami Tourism Bureau - Kinomiya Jinja] * {{Cultural Heritage Online|22_shizuoka|7274|Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property: Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori}} {{Shinto Navbox}} {{Shinto-stub}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{translated page|ja|来宮神社|version=104107598|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 7]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Shizuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:History of Atami]] [[Category:Yamato Takeru]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Son-sha]] [[Category:Atami, Shizuoka]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:everybodywiki import successful]][[Category:everybodywiki import successful]] }} [[Category:Everybody linked]] {{everybodywiki link|Kinomiya Shrine}} [[Category:Yamato Takeru]] [[Category:Buildings in Atami]] [[Category:History of Atami]] [[Category:Son-sha in Shizuoka Prefecture]] {{Commons category|Kinomiya-jinja}} [[ja:来宮神社]] [[zh:來宮神社]] {{wikidata link|Q11523682}}

Its festival, the Kogashi Matsuri (below), is Atami’s largest festival. It also performs rituals for many other shrines in Atami City that do not have their own resident priest. Only Izusan Jinja, Imamiya Jinja, and Ajiko Jinja have their own priests. Other shrines such as Misogino Taki Jinja, Meisui Jinja, Danna Jinja, Fujimori Inari Jinja, Yunomae Jinja, Goten Inari Jinja, Dairokuten-son Jinja, Tagajinja, Shimotaga Jinja, Tsushima Jinja, Koyama Shinmeigū, Wadanoki Jinja, and others are served by Kinomiya Jinja’s priests. Wada Hachiman Jinja’s rites are conducted by Imamiya Jinja’s priest, and Hatsuki Jinja on Hatsushima (an offshore island of Atami) is served by Izusan Jinja’s priest. As Atami’s tourism fortunes waned after the Bubble Economy collapse, pilgrimages to Kinomiya Jinja also declined. However, as Atami tourism recovered in the 2010s, Kinomiya Jinja also saw an increase in visitors. They introduced selfie stands, an open cafe, walking guides, and collaborated with local shops to create new sweets. In 2017, about 688,000 people visited, over four times the roughly 157,000 in 2008.[https://mainichi.jp/articles/20181203/dde/001/040/033000c “Check: Rebound with a Sacred Camphor Tree—Kinomiya Jinja in Atami leverages youth and female appeal”], Mainichi Shimbun (Evening edition), December 3, 2018, p.1. Accessed December 7, 2018. == Main festivals == === Kogashi Matsuri === * festival “Kogashi Matsuri” held around July 15 (including the eve on July 14 and events through July 16). Originally, as old lunar calendar June 15 was the day the fishermen discovered the wooden deity, they held the festival then, but in Meiji times it changed to the solar calendar.[http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/reitaisai.html festival] Kinomiya Jinja official site ** July 14: Eve festival (Yoi-miya-sai), praying for successful ceremonies. ** July 15: festival “Kogashi Matsuri” *** “Miya Mikoshi Togyo” (9:00–15:00): The shrine’s mikoshi visits Atami Station, Shinsui Park, Ginza-chō, and other city areas. *** “Reitaisai Hōhei” (11:00–): Offerings of mugikogashi (roasted barley flour), lily bulbs, bitter oranges, and tokoro jelly according to tradition. *** “Hōshuku Shinnei Gishiki” (11:40–13:00): Kashima Odori (Kashima dance), Miko Kagura (shrine maiden dance), Urayasu no Mai. *** “Kogashi Matsuri Dashi Contest” (18:30–21:30): About 30+ festival floats line up on National Route 135, which is closed off near Hotel Ōnoya through Atami Sun Beach, competing in a parade-style contest. ** July 16: *** “Jinkō-sai” (Shinkō-sai) **** “Hōshuku Shinnei Gishiki” (8:30–): Kashima Odori, Miko Kagura, Urayasu no Mai **** “Goshinkō Gyōretsu” (9:50–15:40): A procession of about 500 people including Tengu-masked, high-geta wearing Sarutahiko distributing mugikogashi (symbolizing rice), a Mikoshi, Shishimai (lion dance), priests, etc. They visit Yunomae Jinja, Atami Station, Sun Beach (with a mikoshi purification), Nagisa Kōen (with dances), and Ginza. At Ginza (in front of Ozawa Himono-ten[http://atamii.jp/today/73259/ Goshinkō parade in Atami city by Kinomiya Jinja concluding festival], Atami Net News, 2017/7/17), Kashima Odori is also performed. **** “Kanchōsai” (15:40–) *** “Kogashi Matsuri Dashi Contest” (18:30–21:00) === Setsubun festival === On Setsubun (February 3), a lively bean-throwing ceremony takes place with participating celebrities. Past participants include: * Izumi Pinko * Ehara Hiroyuki * Kuroda Arthur * Satō Yōko (violinist) * Nishikido Oyakata (former sumo wrestler Mitoizumi Masato) * Hashida Sugako * Hayashi Mariko * Motoki Daisuke == Shrine Buildings == The honden is nagare-zukuri style, connected with heiden and haiden in a gongen-zukuri arrangement. == Subsidiary Shrines == Within the precincts: * Kinomiya Inari-sha (Inari shrine from Fushimi Inari Taisha in Kyoto) * Kinomiya Benzaiten (Benzaiten statue by Takamura Kōun is shown on November 23) * Mitsumine Jinja [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/top/setsumassha.html Kinomiya Jinja – Subsidiary Shrines] (Accessed December 7, 2018) == Cultural Properties == [[File:Azusawake Jinja no Okusu -02.jpg|thumb|150px|Great Camphor Tree of Azusawake Jinja]] === National Natural Monument === {{Main|{{ill|Azusawake Jinja no Ōkusu|ja|阿豆佐和気神社の大クス|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Azusawake Jinja no Ōkusu|1=Azusawakejinja-no-Okusu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q60403026}}|{{ill|Kamanariya Heishichi|ja|釜鳴屋平七|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamanariya Heishichi|1=kamanariya heishichi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q65289080}}}} * The Great Camphor Tree of Azusawake Jinja (over 2000 years old, trunk circumference about 24m, height 20m), designated in Shōwa 8. Circling it once is said to extend life by one year or grant wishes. Historically, seven camphor trees stood here, but during the Ansei era (1855–60), a dispute related to fishing rights (the Ōami/maguro-ami incident) forced them to cut five for lawsuit costs.[https://www.city.atami.lg.jp/kosodate/shogaigakushu/1011165/1006016/1009091/1009107.html Episode 14: Local Hero Kamanariya Heishichi] - Atami City Hall[http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/supporting_party/ 50th Anniversary of Iitakeru no Mikoto’s 1300th Enshrinement: Rebuilding Senshūden and Grounds Improvement Project] - Kinomiya Jinja Another large camphor stands near the entrance. === Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property === * Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori (Kashima dance) Performed during the Kogashi Matsuri at the shrine grounds, Atami Station front, Nagisa Kōen, and Ginza Street. The dancers carry ladles with colored papers symbolizing rice grains, praying for abundant harvest and warding off evil. It’s recognized as a Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property. == Trees == Horuto-no-ki ([[:en:Elaeocarpus sylvestris|Elaeacarpus sylvestris var. ellipticus]]): A unique evergreen species rare to Japan. Characterized by smooth gray bark and leathery leaves, it produces white flowers in July or August. Its leaves turn red before shedding. Two species of this genus grow wild in the warm temperate regions of Japan. Kinomiya no O-kusu (Camphor Tree, Cinnamomum camphora): This colossal tree, standing 23 meters in circumference and estimated to be over 2,000 years old, is recognized as Japan's second largest and oldest kusunoki tree. Known as Goshinboku, or the Holy Tree, it's believed that a Shinto god resides within it. Many believe the tree possesses special powers, granting health, safety, and longevity to those who visit. The bark of this tree is brown and lightly fissured, and its wood is often used in furniture and sculpture. Extracts from the leaves of this tree have medicinal uses in Chinese medicine. It is designated as a natural monument. == Other natural treasures == Beyond the Kinomiya Shrine, other notable trees include Japan's largest camphor tree located at a Hachiman Shrine in Kamo-cho, Kagoshima, and the oldest tree in Japan, a 3,000-year-old kusunoki found in Saga Prefecture. The Kinomiya Shrine is surrounded by a woodland which can be classified as a small laurel forest or ''shoyo-juinrin''. Many trees in this forest are broadleaf evergreens, safeguarding aspects of the local flora from development. == Other == * In May 2011, a 300-year-old holly oak tree next to the torii toppled at its base and damaged the 1920s torii. == Access == * About a 5-minute walk from [[:en:Kinomiya Station|Kinomiya Station]] (JR Itō Line). Also walkable (about 18 minutes) from [[:en:Atami Station|Atami Station]] or reachable by city bus (Ten Nation Pass line or Nishiyama loop) to “Kinomiya Jinja Mae” bus stop.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=http://kinomiya.or.jp/top/praying/access/|title=Access|publisher=Kinomiya Jinja|accessdate=2021-04-21}} The shrine grounds are open from 9:00 to 17:00. == References == * Tanigawa Ken’ichi ed., "Nihon no Kami, Jinja to Seichi Vol.10 Tōkai", Hakusuisha, 1987 == See Also == * Kinomiya faith * Kashima Odori == Notes == === Notes === {{notelist}} === Sources === {{Reflist|2}} == External Links == {{commonscat|Kinomiya-jinja}} * [http://www.kinomiya.or.jp/ Official Website of Kinomiya Jinja] * [https://atami.travel/atami-tourism/kinomiya-shrin/ Atami Tourism Bureau - Kinomiya Jinja] * {{Cultural Heritage Online|22_shizuoka|7274|Shizuoka Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property: Kinomiya Jinja Kashima Odori}} {{Shinto Navbox}} {{Shinto-stub}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{translated page|ja|来宮神社|version=104107598|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 7]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Shizuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:History of Atami]] [[Category:Yamato Takeru]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Son-sha]] [[Category:Atami, Shizuoka]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:everybodywiki import successful]][[Category:everybodywiki import successful]] }} [[Category:Everybody linked]] {{everybodywiki link|Kinomiya Shrine}} [[Category:Yamato Takeru]] [[Category:Buildings in Atami]] [[Category:History of Atami]] [[Category:Son-sha in Shizuoka Prefecture]] {{Commons category|Kinomiya-jinja}} [[ja:来宮神社]] [[zh:來宮神社]] {{wikidata link|Q11523682}} [[Category:Wikidata has short description]]
